35.0 Decoding plant responses to herbivory: the emerging role of extracellular ATP and purinergic receptors.
Yadav MN, Meena MK.
reviewKinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunityPlant cell reports · 2026-11-05
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, Rboh*, apoplast*, annexin*, CPK*, extracellular ATP, eATP, DORN1, P2K1, MAPK*, signaling
abstract

Key messageWe summarize how eATP serves as a key DAMP molecule during herbivory and contributes to plant defense responses. Perception of tissue damage during insect herbivory is a critical step in activating plant defense responses. Extracellular ATP (eATP) has emerged as an important damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) that links herbivore-induced tissue damage to early signaling events and downstream defense responses. This review summarizes the mechanisms underlying the release and accumulation of eATP in the apoplast during insect herbivory and mechanical wounding. It considers elicitor-induced and developmental processes that regulate eATP signaling. We discuss how eATP released during herbivore-induced tissue damage is perceived primarily by the plasma membrane receptor P2K1/DORN1 and activates Ca2⁺, reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide (NO), MAPK, and CPK signaling cascades involved in herbivore-induced defense. Specific emphasis is placed on integrating eATP signaling with jasmonate and different phytohormone pathways that regulate herbivore-responsive defense, as well as on emerging mechanisms that control the amplification, modulation, and attenuation of eATP signaling during insect attack. We further examine how eATP-associated signaling contributes to transcriptional reprogramming, accumulation of defense proteins, secondary metabolite production, and structural defense responses during herbivory. Modern advances linking eATP signaling with additional regulatory components, including RBOHs, FERONIA, annexins, MVK, and PAT5/PAT9, are also discussed. Finally, we highlight major knowledge gaps and future research directions, and discuss potential biotechnological strategies to manipulate eATP-associated signaling to enhance crop resistance to insect herbivores while maintaining plant growth and productivity.

25.0 A calcium-dependent BAK1-GLR-TPC1-CBP60g-ICS1 module underlies salicylic acid accumulation during whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) feeding in Arabidopsis.
Zhang FB, Han WH, Liu YX … Wang XW.
Kinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunityJournal of advanced research · 2026-11-09
matched: calcium, calcium signal*, GLR*, glutamate receptor-like, calmodulin*, kinase*, receptor kinase*, signaling, receptor*, salicylic acid, brassinosteroid*, phytohormone*
abstract

IntroductionPiercing-sucking insects such as whiteflies trigger salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defenses despite causing minimal tissue damage. Although SA accumulation is a hallmark of plant responses to these herbivores, the upstream signaling mechanisms linking insect perception to SA biosynthesis remain poorly understood, particularly in the context of herbivore-associated molecular patterns (HAMPs) and calcium signaling.ObjectivesThis study aims to elucidate the molecular pathway connecting whitefly feeding to SA accumulation, focusing on the roles of calcium signaling components, transcriptional regulators, and SA biosynthetic enzymes.MethodsUsing Arabidopsis thaliana, we combined genetic, molecular, and biochemical approaches. SA levels and gene expression were quantified in wild-type and mutant lines (sid2-2, sid2, cbp60g, sard1, bak1, glr3.3/3.6, tpc1) following whitefly infestation. Calcium dynamics were monitored using aequorin-based reporters. Insect performance assays were conducted to evaluate plant resistance.ResultsWhitefly feeding significantly induced SA accumulation and PR1 expression in wild-type plants. This response depended on ISOCHORISMATE SYNTHASE 1 (ICS1), as sid2 mutants failed to accumulate SA. The transcription factor CALMODULIN-BINDING PROTEIN 60 g (CBP60g) positively regulates ICS1 expression and SA production. Furthermore, calcium signaling components, including BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1-ASSOCIATED RECEPTOR KINASE 1 (BAK1), GLUTAMATE RECEPTOR-LIKE 3.3 and 3.6 (GLR3.3/GLR3.6), and TWO-PORE CHANNEL 1 (TPC1), were required for full activation of ICS1 expression and SA accumulation. Mutations in these components impaired defense responses and enhanced whitefly performance. Collectively, these elements form a signaling module linking insect perception to SA biosynthesis.ConclusionWe identified a BAK1-GLR-TPC1-CBP60g-ICS1 signaling module governing SA accumulation upon whitefly feeding. This pathway highlights the central role of calcium signaling in transducing insect feeding-associated signals into phytohormone defense responses. Our work provides new insights into plant-insect interactions and identifies conserved signaling nodes that can be exploited as molecular targets for breeding or engineering crops with stronger resistance to piercing-sucking pests.

22.5 Hormone-Mediated Signaling of Reactive Oxygen Species Under Abiotic Stress.
Fedoreyeva LI, Bursakov SA, Molchanova TP … Zakharova EV.
reviewKinases and signal transductionHormonesAbiotic stressInternational journal of molecular sciences · 2026-10-28
matched: Ca2+, ROS, reactive oxygen species, Rboh*, NADPH oxidase*, apoplast*, kinase*, phosphoryl*, signaling, receptor*, auxin*, abscisic acid
abstract

Abiotic stresses trigger the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in various subcellular compartments of plant cells, where they perform a dual function: acting as cytotoxic agents during acute stress and as highly specific signaling modulators under mild or chronic stress. However, the fundamental question of how the cell distinguishes between toxic and signaling ROS pools-and how phytohormones coordinate this distinction-remains unresolved. This review re-examines the molecular logic of the hormone-redox interface, focusing on the post-translational modifications of NADPH oxidases (RBOHs) and antioxidant enzymes as a key mechanism for the rapid tuning of signals. Moving beyond traditional linear cascade models, we propose the concept of a "dynamic hormonal code," in which abscisic acid acts as the primary initiator of apoplastic ROS bursts via SnRK2-dependent phosphorylation, while salicylates and jasmonates modulate the duration and amplitude of these bursts, thereby determining the outcome-ranging from programmed cell death to systemic resistance. Known mechanisms of the hormonal code have been established (e.g., ABA → SnRK2 → RBOH; SA/JA antagonism mediated by NPR1; and the redox relay involving PRXIIB/GPX3 → ABI2). This review goes beyond simple hormone combinatorics by proposing a conceptual framework: the hormonal code encodes ROS signals through parameters of time, amplitude, and cellular compartment. Particular attention is paid to recent discoveries regarding the roles of auxin and brassinosteroids in reconfiguring chloroplast redox homeostasis during flooding and heat shock. Generalizing these data, we propose an integrated model of spatiotemporal regulation that explains how feedback loops involving ROS, Ca2+ waves, and hormone receptors facilitate systemic acclimation. Thus, targeting key crosstalk nodes-specifically SnRK2 and TOR kinase complexes-offers new strategies for engineering stress-resilient crops in the face of climate change.

21.5 The Maize Calcium-Binding Protein ZmCML36 Positively Regulates Tolerance to Drought and Salt Stress.
Zhang Z, Bao P, Zhang X … Qi X.
Kinases and signal transductionAbiotic stressCell biology and organellesPlants (Basel, Switzerland) · 2026-11-02
matched: calcium, Ca2+, calmodulin*, CML*, signaling, salt stress, salinity, drought, stress respon*, nuclear, roots, germination
abstract

Drought and salinity severely limit maize (Zea mays L.) production worldwide. Calcium (Ca2+) signaling is central to plant stress responses, but the functions of many calcium sensors, including calmodulin-like proteins (CMLs), remain poorly understood in maize. Here, we characterized ZmCML36 as a positive regulator of drought and salt stress tolerance. Transcriptional analysis showed that ZmCML36 was strongly induced by drought and salt treatments. Overexpression of ZmCML36 in Arabidopsis and maize enhanced stress tolerance, as indicated by higher germination rates, longer roots, increased superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, and reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) content. Conversely, an EMS-derived ZmCML36 mutant exhibited greater stress sensitivity. Transient expression analysis showed ZmCML36-GFP fluorescence at the cell periphery and nuclear region. An in vitro mobility-shift assay supported the Ca2+-binding capacity of ZmCML36. A yeast two-hybrid screen, followed by luciferase complementation imaging in Nicotiana benthamiana, identified an interaction between ZmCML36 and Zm00001eb395720, a putative regulatory β subunit of the maize SnRK1 complex. These findings suggest a potential connection between Ca2+ signaling and SnRK1-associated energy regulation during abiotic stress responses and identify ZmCML36 as a candidate gene for improving abiotic stress tolerance in maize.

19.5 The WRKY transcription factor NtWRKY11 confers cold tolerance in tobacco via an ABA-associated regulatory pathway.
Luo Y, Feng L, Geng Z … Jia H.
Kinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunityPlant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology · 2026-11-13
matched: calcium, calcium signal*, ROS, reactive oxygen species, CNGC*, CPK*, signaling, ABA, defense, drought, cold stress, nuclear
abstract

WRKY transcription factors contribute substantially to plant responses toward diverse abiotic stresses. Nevertheless, little is known regarding the molecular mechanism of tobacco NtWRKY11 under cold stress conditions. Herein, we identified that NtWRKY11, a nuclear-localized transcription factor, is markedly induced by cold and drought stresses. Overexpression of NtWRKY11 significantly improved tobacco cold tolerance, as evidenced by reduced electrolyte leakage, lower reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, higher seed-germination rate, and better-maintained photosynthetic capacity under cold stress. Transcriptome and physiological analyses revealed that NtWRKY11 may promotes the transcription of ABA biosynthetic genes NCED3 and AAO3, facilitating endogenous ABA accumulation under cold stress. NtWRKY11-associated ABA may further modulate CNGC-mediated calcium signaling. Both ABA and calcium-CPK signaling converge and may modulate the CBF-COR regulatory module. Meanwhile, NtWRKY11 enhances antioxidant defense by up-regulating antioxidant-related genes and elevating antioxidant‑enzyme activities. Collectively, NtWRKY11 confers enhanced cold tolerance in tobacco by coordinating ABA-associated calcium signaling, the CBF-COR cold-responsive cascade and antioxidant defense systems.

Abstract Rice ( Oryza sativa L.) is a staple food crop in China, where salt stress poses a severe constraint on rice growth and development. Prohexadione calcium (Pro-Ca) has been recognized as an effective regulator in mitigating salt stress damage in rice. In this pot experiment, two rice cultivars—the salt-sensitive Huanghuazhan (HHZ) and the salt-tolerant Guanghong No. 3 (GH3)—were used as plant materials. Foliar application of Pro-Ca was conducted at the three-leaf stage, followed by NaCl treatment at the four-leaf stage. Three treatments were established: (1) 0 mM NaCl + 0 mg·L -1 Pro-Ca (control, CK); (2) 70 mM NaCl + 0 mg·L -1 Pro-Ca (salt stress, S); (3) 70 mM NaCl + 100 mg·L -1 Pro-Ca (salt stress + Pro-Ca, SP). On day 11 after NaCl exposure, untargeted lipidomics profiling was performed. Chloroplast ultrastructure was observed via transmission electron microscopy on day 21, and photosynthetic gas exchange parameters 【net photosynthetic rate(Pn), intercellular CO₂ concentration ༈Ci༉, stomatal conductance༈Gs༉, transpiration rate ༈Tr) and photosynthetic pigment concentrations (chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids, total chlorophyll)】 were quantified on day 31 after salt treatment. The underlying mechanism by which Pro-Ca alleviates salt stress-induced damage was elucidated based on the sequential alterations in lipid metabolites, chloroplast ultrastructure, and photosynthetic function.Our results revealed that at the lipid metabolic level, GH3 exhibited a much stronger lipidomic response to salt stress than HHZ, with 283 and 35 differentially accumulated lipids identified, respectively. GH3 showed coordinated remodeling across multiple lipid classes, including dysregulated galactolipids (up-regulated DGDG and partially down-regulated MGDG), reduced phospholipids, and accumulated glycerolipids. By contrast, the lipid response in HHZ was dominated solely by the passive accumulation of glycerolipids (TG and DG). At the chloroplast ultrastructural level, HHZ chloroplasts displayed more severe disintegration of thylakoid lamellae and greater accumulation of osmiophilic plastoglobules, whereas GH3 chloroplasts retained better overall morphology and intact grana architecture. With respect to photosynthetic performance, HHZ was characterized by a marked decline in stomatal parameters accompanied by only a minor reduction in photosynthetic pigment contents, while GH3 exhibited substantial degradation of photosynthetic pigments.Our findings demonstrated that foliar application of Pro-Ca conferred stepwise alleviation of salt stress damage via the regulation of leaf lipid homeostasis. Specifically, Pro-Ca first prioritized the remodeling of leaf lipid profiles and restored membrane lipid composition by modulating glycerolipid metabolism and phospholipid biosynthesis pathways. This lipidomic remodeling subsequently facilitated the restoration of ordered thylakoid grana stacking, reduced the accumulation of osmiophilic plastoglobules, and preserved chloroplast structural integrity. Ultimately, these improvements translated into elevated photosynthetic gas exchange parameters and photosynthetic pigment contents, thereby mitigating salt-induced photosynthetic damage.Notably, the alleviatory effects of Pro-Ca exhibited pronounced genotype specificity. In HHZ, Pro-Ca predominantly targeted the clearance of excess accumulated glycerolipids, leading to a comprehensive recovery of all eight measured photosynthetic traits. 14.0 Functional Analysis of GarCIPK8 from Gossypium aridum Conferring Salt Stress Tolerance in Gossypium hirsutum.
Guo Q, Tao J, Lv J … Xu Z.
Kinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunityPlants (Basel, Switzerland) · 2026-11-01
matched: calcium, Ca2+, CBL*, CIPK*, kinase*, signal transduction, signaling, hormone*, defense, salt stress, NaCl, stress respon*
abstract

Soil salinization is a major abiotic stress factor restricting global agricultural production. The CBL-CIPK signaling network, comprising calcineurin B-like proteins (CBLs) and CBL-interacting protein kinases (CIPKs), plays a critical role in plant adaptation to salt stress. Here, we focused on GarCIPK8, a CIPK gene previously isolated from the diploid wild cotton Gossypium aridum, and generated its overexpressing transgenic lines in G. hirsutum through Agrobacterium-mediated transformation. Under 300 mmol/L NaCl treatment, transgenic plants showed markedly enhanced growth performance, with greater height and biomass accumulation than the wild type, and these differences increased with the duration of salt exposure, reaching a maximum at 30 d. This phenotypic advantage was associated with enhanced activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and peroxidase (POD), together with significantly reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) content. Specifically, at 3 d of salt stress, the transgenic lines exhibited significantly higher SOD activity than the wild type, while POD activity was markedly higher at both 1 d and 3 d. Ion content analysis revealed distinct distribution patterns between transgenic and wild-type plants. At 3 d and 7 d, transgenic roots accumulated significantly less Na+, whereas Na+ content in stems and leaves was substantially higher. In parallel, at 15 d, the transgenic lines showed significantly elevated root and stem K+ levels, as well as increased root Ca2+ content at the early stage of salt treatment (1 d and 3 d). Transcriptomic analysis further supported these phenotypic and physiological changes, as differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were significantly enriched in Gene Ontology (GO) terms related to antioxidant activity, peroxidase activity, and oxidative stress response, as well as in Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways including calcium ion binding, metal ion transport, transporter activity, ABC transporters, and plant hormone signal transduction. These results demonstrate that GarCIPK8 enhances salt tolerance in G. hirsutum by synergistically regulating ion homeostasis and antioxidant defense, providing a valuable genetic resource for cotton breeding.

13.5 Complementary protective effects of autophagy and antioxidative activity on salt tolerance in Suaeda salsa seedlings.
Deng L, Feng Y, Cheng H … Li H.
Abiotic stressCell biology and organellesGrowthBMC plant biology · 2026-08-14
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, H2O2, salt stress, salinity, autophagy, root, shoot*, seed*, microscop*
abstract

BackgroundSoil salinity is a major concern for agricultural productivity worldwide. The halophyte Suaeda salsa can survive in saline environments, and the timely removal of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by plants is critical for enhancing salt tolerance. However, the mechanisms underlying salt tolerance in S. salsa remain unclear. In this study, we investigated the relationships among autophagy, antioxidant enzyme activity, and ROS accumulation in S. salsa under salt stress.ResultsThe root/shoot ratio of S. salsa desreased as salt concentration increased, whereas dry weight and polysaccharide content remained relatively high under saline conditions. Under 200 mM sodium chloride treatment, S. salsa exhibited the strongest superoxide anion radical and hydroxyl radical scavenging capacities, along with the lowest H2O2 content. Transmission electron microscopy revealed basal autophagy under 200 mM sodium chlorid. Superoxide dismutase activity remained high under salt stress, while the activities of catalase and peroxidase were highest in the salt-free control. Transcriptome analysis showed that the expression profiles of key genes were broadly consistent with changes in enzyme activity and autophagy. Correlation analysis further indicated that both antioxidant enzyme activity and autophagy were associated with free radical scavenging. Superoxide anion radical scavenging ability was negatively correlated with Atg8, Pod, and Cat; hydroxyl radical scavenging ability was positively correlated with Sod, and H2O2 content was positively correlated with Cwm.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that autophagy and antioxidative enzymes act in a coorrdinated protective network during S. salsa adaptation to salt stress, providing a theoretical foundation for future work on regulating salt tolerance.

13.0 MdMYB1R1 Activates MdMAPKKK18 and Additional Defense Pathways to Confer Resistance to Woody Fungal Pathogens in Apple.
Liu H, Chen S, Zhang Q … Huang L.
Kinases and signal transductionPlant-microbe interactions and immunityCell biology and organellesPlant, cell & environment · 2026-11-10
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, kinase*, MAPK*, signaling, pathogen*, defense, nucleus, woody, reporter*, luciferase*
abstract

Trunk diseases caused by woody plant pathogens, including Valsa mali and Botryosphaeria dothidea, represent a major threat to global apple production; however, the molecular basis of host resistance remains largely elusive. In this study, we employed TMT-based quantitative proteomic profiling to compare necrotic and uninfected twig tissues of apple following V. mali inoculation, identifying 904 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs). Among these, the MYB transcription factor, MdMYB1R1, exhibited a pronounced induction in response to pathogen infection. Subcellular localization and transactivation assays revealed that MdMYB1R1 localizes to the nucleus and acts as a transcriptional activator. Transient overexpression of MdMYB1R1 in Nicotiana benthamiana potentiated reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and activated MAPK signaling, correlating with enhanced resistance against Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. Stable overexpression of MdMYB1R1 in apple markedly enhanced resistance to both V. mali and B. dothidea, whereas silencing of MdMYB1R1 impaired disease tolerance. Through DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq), yeast one-hybrid (Y1H), electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA), and dual-luciferase reporter assays, we demonstrated that MdMYB1R1 binds to the promoter region of MdMAPKKK18 and activates its transcription, a gene encoding a mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase involved in MAPK signaling. Genetic epistasis analysis further revealed that overexpression of MdMAPKKK18 only partially rescued the compromised resistance in MdMYB1R1-RNAi plants. Collectively, our findings identify MdMYB1R1 as a key positive regulator of apple resistance against trunk fungal diseases, acting at least in part by directly activating the MdMAPKKK18-mediated MAPK cascade and by regulating additional defense pathways, thus providing a promising candidate for breeding disease-resistant apple cultivars.

13.0 ROS-dependent phosphorylation of insulin receptor and insulin receptor substrate during pupal diapause development in the cotton bollworm, Helicoverpa armigera.
Su Z, Yang Y, Ke Y … Jiang S.
Kinases and signal transductionAbiotic stressGrowthInsect science · 2026-11-11
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, kinase*, phosphoryl*, signaling, receptor*, ubiquitin*, stress respon*, growth, development
abstract

Insect diapause is a critical adaptive strategy characterized by developmental arrest and enhanced stress tolerance, orchestrated by intricate molecular networks. The insulin signaling pathway, which governs growth, metabolism, and stress responses, has been implicated in diapause regulation. However, the precise roles of insulin receptor (InR) and insulin receptor substrate (IRS) in modulating pupal diapause remain incompletely understood, particularly in the economically important pest Helicoverpa armigera. Here, we show that InR and IRS are associated with pupal diapause development through redox-sensitive phosphorylation cascades. Temporal profiling revealed a marked upregulation of phosphorylated InR (p-InR) and IRS (p-IRS) in diapause-destined pupal brains, concomitant with elevated phosphorylation of Akt (p-Akt) and ERK (p-ERK). Functional validation in Helicoverpa zea (HzAm1) cells, via overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi), showed that IRS positively regulates Akt and ERK signaling. Further mechanistic studies indicated that reactive oxygen species (ROS) act upstream of the phosphorylation of InR, IRS, Akt, and ERK in vitro and in vivo; these effects were reversible upon ROS scavenging. Further investigations revealed that increased p-ERK was associated with global protein ubiquitination, suggesting this kinase as a key regulator of proteasomal degradation in diapause development. Our findings delineate a ROS-InR-IRS-Akt/ERK signaling framework associated with diapause development and proteostatic regulation in H. armigera, thereby advancing our understanding of insect diapause biology and providing candidate molecular targets for future pest-management interventions.

13.0 Unlocking the three-node regulatory axis: polyamines, antioxidants, and photosynthetic protection in stressed fruit crops.
Jan M, Aucique-Perez CE, Mattia M … Shahid MA.
reviewKinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunityFrontiers in plant science · 2026-10-21
matched: H2O2, hydrogen peroxide, MAPK*, signaling, ethylene, hormone*, defense, salinity, drought, stress respon*, chloroplast*, stoma*
abstract

Abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity, heat, and cold, disrupt cellular redox homeostasis and impair photosynthesis in fruit crops, directly threatening vegetative growth, fruit set, and marketable yield. While polyamines (PAs), mainly putrescine, spermidine, and spermine, are well-known mediators of environmental stress tolerance, their precise molecular roles in fruit crops remain fragmented. This review conceptualizes PA-mediated stress tolerance through a novel "three-node regulatory axis". The first node governs cellular PA homeostasis through a tightly coordinated network of biosynthesis (via arginine decarboxylase [ADC], S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase [SAMDC], and spermidine/spermine synthases [SPDS/SPMS]) and catabolism (via diamine and polyamine oxidases [DAO/PAO]). The second node involves antioxidant activation, where controlled PA catabolism generates signaling levels of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) that prime enzymatic and non-enzymatic defense mechanisms and preserve cellular and chloroplast redox poise. Beyond direct antioxidant activation, PA-dependent redox signals can interface with Ca²+-dependent pathways, MAPK cascades, nitric oxide, and hormone signaling to regulate stress-responsive gene expression. The third node encompasses photosynthetic protection, maintaining thylakoid membrane stability, protecting photosystem II (PSII) from photoinhibition, regulating stomatal behavior, and supporting carbon assimilation under stress. Although the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana provides a valuable reference framework, direct molecular extrapolation to fruit crops is limited. Fruit crops retain the ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) pathway (which is absent in Brassicaceae), undergo complex perennial woody growth, exhibit fruit-specific hormone crosstalk (particularly PA-ethylene interactions during ripening), and face prolonged field stress conditions. Currently, critical molecular gaps remain in fruit crop research, particularly regarding the direct regulation of Calvin cycle gene expression (such as Rubisco, GAPDH, and SBPase), the functional characterization and regulation of PA transport systems across fruit crops, the direct validation of chloroplast-localized PA biosynthesis, and the upstream transcription factor modules coordinating these responses. To transition the field from physiological association to causal molecular mechanism, future research must prioritize time-resolved, multi-endpoint experimental designs integrating PA profiling, gas exchange, and transcriptomic or proteomic analyses in identical plant systems combined with long-term field evaluation to translate these physiological insights into robust, climate-resilient fruit production.

12.5 Exogenous trehalose mitigates cadmium stress-induced reduction in proline, photosynthesis, and ROS pathways in okra (Abelmoschus esculentus L.) plants.
Pei B, Cao J, Liu T … Wang F.
Abiotic stressGrowthPhysiology and molecular biology of plants : an international journal of functional plant biology · 2026-10-14
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, H2O2, hydrogen peroxide, heavy metal*, cadmium, growth
abstract

Trehalose (Tre) is crucial for metabolic regulation and abiotic stress tolerance in many organisms. However, its role in cadmium (Cd) stress tolerance, particularly through external Tre application, is not well understood. This study explores the physiological and biochemical mechanisms by which Tre enhances Cd stress tolerance in okra. Under CdCl2 stress, okra plants treated with 10 mM Tre demonstrated enhanced growth, with fresh weight (FW) and dry weight (DW) increasing by 123% and 213%, respectively, while untreated plants died during the experiment. Okra plants treated with 10 mM Tre, 5 mM Diphenyleneiodonium (DPI), and a combination of both showed improved growth and increased size, with FW and DW rising by 146%, 136%, 110%, and 385%, 365%, 309%, respectively, under CdCl2 stress. Tre treatment elevated levels of trehalose, proline, photosynthetic pigments, glutathione (GSH), and ascorbic acid (AsA), while reducing hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), malondialdehyde (MDA), and electrolyte leakage. Enzyme activities, including superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GPX), catalase (CAT), glutathione reductase (GR), ascorbate peroxidase (APX), and peroxidase (POD), increased in Tre-treated plants. Under Cd stress, Tre, DPI, and Tre+DPI plants decreased H2O2, superoxide radicals (O2 -), and MDA, with increased CAT, GR, APX, GSH, and AsA in the ASA-GSH cycle. Hierarchical cluster and correlation analyses reveal that exogenous Tre boosts Cd tolerance by regulating osmotic substances, protecting photosynthetic machinery, and activating reactive oxygen species scavenging. Results highlight Tre's key role in enhancing plant resistance to heavy metal stress, suggesting new strategies for improving crop productivity in contaminated environments.

12.5 From stomatal movements to immunity and long-distance signaling: Ion channels mark the spot.
Costa A, Feijó JA, Schroeder JI.
reviewKinases and signal transductionPlant-microbe interactions and immunityAbiotic stressCurrent opinion in plant biology · 2026-11-12
matched: membrane potential, mechanosens*, phosphoryl*, signaling, immun*, nutrient*, stoma*, development, live-cell imaging
abstract

Beyond their established role in mineral nutrition, ion channels have been increasingly recognized as central hubs of plant signaling across multiple scales. Early research revealed functions in stomatal regulation and nutrient transport, with recent breakthroughs highlighting their critical involvement in immunity, development, and long-distance signaling via membrane potential dynamics and diverse ion fluxes. Multiple channels have been characterized as ligand, voltage, or mechanosensitive gated, often modulated by phosphorylation, effectively functioning as integrative hubs of defined stimuli. Structural characterization is now complementing electrophysiology, live-cell imaging, and mass spectrometry, allowing new levels of mechanistic characterization of ion channels in the context of signaling networks and offering new opportunities to engineer plant resilience to stress.

12.5 Molecular mechanisms underlying plant adaptation to low potassium stress.
Liang J, Niu F.
reviewKinases and signal transductionCell biology and organellesGrowthPlant physiology and biochemistry : PPB · 2026-11-04
matched: calcium, calcium signal*, CBL*, CIPK*, signaling, plasma membrane, tonoplast, growth, development
abstract

Potassium (K+) is an essential macronutrient and the most abundant inorganic cation in plant cells. Efficient acquisition, allocation, and homeostatic maintenance of K+ are critical for plant growth, development, and stress tolerance. However, K+ availability in soils is often limited and highly variable, necessitating sophisticated adaptive mechanisms to maintain K+ homeostasis under Low K+ (LK) stress. Over the past decade, substantial progress has been made in dissecting the molecular regulatory networks that govern plant responses to LK stress. Here, we review recent advances in the two central K+ uptake systems, the Shaker-type channel Arabidopsis K+ Transporter 1 (AKT1) and High-Affinity K+ Transporter 5 (HAK5). We further summarize the CBL-CIPK calcium-signaling network as a central hub for decoding LK signals. It operates through sequential activation of a tonoplast-localized CBL2/3-CIPK module and a plasma membrane-localized CBL1/9-CIPK23 module. This temporal ordering is supported by the earlier activation of the tonoplast module, which is itself required for the full activation of the plasma membrane module. We highlight its newly discovered antagonistic crosstalk with the target of rapamycin complex (TORC) growth pathway, which couples K+ status to the balance between growth and stress adaptation. We further present an expanding transcriptional regulatory network, with particular attention to the functional roles of newly identified transcription factors in modulating LK responses. We also discuss conserved and distinct regulatory mechanisms characterized in major cereal and economic crops. Together, these post-translational and transcriptional mechanisms clarify how plants sense and adapt to potassium deficiency, and offer theoretical guidance and candidate genetic targets for breeding potassium-efficient crop varieties.

11.5 N-Hydroxypipecolic Acid Triggers Systemic Acquired Resistance Against Leaf Rust (Puccinia triticina) in Wheat
Sun, S., Formby … G.
preprintKinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunitybioRxiv · 2026-11-15
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, signaling, jasmon*, salicylic acid, immun*, effector*, pathogen*, leaf, leaves
abstract

Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) represents a conserved immune strategy enabling plants to mount long-lasting, whole-plant protection following localized pathogen challenge. In Arabidopsis thaliana, SAR is orchestrated by the mobile immune regulator N-hydroxypipecolic acid (NHP); however, the extent to which NHP defines systemic immune states in polyploid crops remains unclear. Here, we establish NHP as an inducer of systemic immunity in hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum) during infection by the obligate biotrophic fungus Puccinia triticina. Local NHP application conferred robust disease suppression in distal leaves and elicited a temporally structured oxidative response characterized by a distal, biphasic reactive oxygen species (ROS) wave linking local and systemic tissues. RNA-sequencing analysis revealed that NHP induces coordinated transcriptional reprogramming, characterized by systemic activation of pattern-triggered and effector-triggered immunity pathways, WRKY-centered transcriptional networks, NPR1-associated signaling, and broad-spectrum resistance loci including Lr34. Concomitantly, targeted metabolomic profiling revealed a unique systemic accumulation of salicylic acid, salicylic acid glucoside, pipecolic acid, and NHP, without the conventional jasmonate signaling antagonism observed in eudicots. Despite this conserved immune architecture, functional analyses indicated divergence within the NHP biosynthetic pathway; while a single wheat FMO from sub-clade A2 was systemically up-regulated by NHP, the highly conserved TaSARD4 homeologs were constitutively expressed and functionally dispensable for rust resistance in planta. Notably, heterologous expression of TaSARD4-B successfully restored NHP-glucoside accumulation in an Arabidopsis sard4 mutant, confirming biochemical competence and suggesting alternative metabolic redundancies in wheat. These findings define a systems-level NHP-driven immune state in wheat and provide a conceptual framework for dissecting systemic immunity in cereals, extending SAR paradigms beyond model plant systems.

11.5 Nodulation induces systemic defense in Phaseolus vulgaris leaves against Sclerotinia sclerotiorum through ROS accumulation and COBRA-like gene expression.
Mora-Carlón BA, Aguilar-Gutiérrez YJ, Chávez-Martínez AI … Sarmiento-López LG.
Plant-microbe interactions and immunityCell biology and organellesGrowthPlanta · 2026-11-13
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, immun*, pathogen*, rhizobi*, symbio*, defense, cell wall*, root, leaves
abstract

Main conclusionMature root nodule symbiosis enhances susceptibility infection to Sclerotinia sclerotiorum by coordinating ROS, defense metabolism, cell-wall carbohydrate profiles, and specific PvCOBL gene responses in Phaseolus vulgaris. Root nodule symbiosis (RNS) enhances plant nutrition and can systemically modify plant defense responses. However, the mechanisms linking RNS to resistance against necrotrophic pathogens remain poorly understood in Phaseolus vulgaris. In this study, we investigated whether nodulation induced by Rhizobium tropici influences systemic resistance to Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and is associated with changes in reactive oxygen species (ROS), defense-related metabolism, cell wall-associated carbohydrates, and COBRA-like (COBL) gene family. A temporal analysis of nodulation (7, 14, 21, and 30 days post inoculation, dpi) revealed that resistance to S. sclerotiorum was strongly dependent on the developmental stage of symbiosis. At the mature nodule stage (21 dpi), nodulated plants (N+) exhibited approximately 7 fold lower necrotic lesion area than non-nodulated (N-) plants, whereas susceptibility was greater at immature (14 dpi) and senescent (30 dpi) stages of nodulation. Enhanced resistance at 21 dpi was associated with a 5-fold increase in H₂O₂ accumulation, elevated phenolic and flavonoid contents, increased chlorophyll levels, and changes in cell wall-associated carbohydrate profiles. Genome-wide analysis identified 14 PvCOBL genes distributed across three phylogenetic clades and revealed substantial conservation in gene structure, and the characteristic CCVS motif. Promoter and transcriptomic analyses revealed that PvCOBL genes exhibit distinct tissue-, developmental-, symbiosis-, and pathogen-associated expression patterns. RT-qPCR further identified PvCOBL9 and PvCOBL10 as promising candidates associated with nodulation-dependent pathogen responses. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that nodule maturation is associated with systemic physiological and transcriptional reprogramming that contributes to reduced susceptibility to S. sclerotiorum. This work provides the first comprehensive characterization of the COBL gene family in P. vulgaris and identifies candidate genes that may link rhizobial symbiosis, cell wall-associated processes, and systemic immunity.

11.5 Plant Cellular Phase Homeostasis: From Cytoplasmic Phase Plasticity to Metabolic Switching, Stress Adaptation, and Recovery
Khablak SH, Bondareva LM, Kolomiiets YV … Abdullaieva YA.
preprintKinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunityPreprints.org · 2026-11-10
matched: Ca²⁺, reactive oxygen species, pH, kinase*, signalling, abscisic acid, hormone*, immun*, stress respon*, autophagy, cell expansion, growth
abstract

Plant stress physiology has produced detailed descriptions of individual pathways—abscisic acid signalling, Ca²⁺ and reactive oxygen species networks, SnRK1 and TOR energy sensing, hormone crosstalk and transcriptional reprogramming—yet it still struggles to explain why the same stress elicits different outcomes in similar cells, why activation of protective pathways does not guarantee survival, and why recovery after stress is often incomplete. Here we argue that a missing integrative variable is the physicochemical state of the cytoplasm itself. We review evidence that cytosolic pH, ionic strength, energy charge, redox poise, macromolecular crowding, hydration and viscosity are regulated, stress-responsive quantities that control the assembly and material state of biomolecular condensates. Plant proteins including FLOE1, ELF3, phytochrome B, SEUSS, DCP5, subgroup I SnRK2 kinases, FUST1, RBGD2/4 and MBS1 sense hydration, temperature, crowding or singlet oxygen directly through phase behaviour, and condensates are now known to activate SnRK1, store and release autophagy proteins and control translation. Building on our previous theory of cytoplasmic phase homeostasis, we propose an integrative framework in which (i) cytoplasmic phase sensing acts as a distributed layer of stress perception; (ii) the phase state is coupled to the FLZ–SnRK1–TOR–autophagy network and may set the threshold and hysteresis of metabolic switching; (iii) the same state gates the mechanochemical capacity for cell expansion beyond the acid growth model; and (iv) the cytoplasmic phase reserve and the recovery trajectory determine resilience. We define six functional states, from the TOR-dominant growth state to adaptive reprogramming, immune–metabolic exhaustion, collapse and recovery, and grade every claim by level of evidence. Eight falsifiable hypotheses, with molecular markers, experimental designs and refutation criteria, are formulated, together with an integrated multiparameter measurement strategy and a prospective Plant Phase Homeostasis Index for resilience phenotyping.

11.5 The Role of Long-Term DNA Replication Stress Induced by Hydroxyurea in Meristematic Root Cells of Allium cepa.
Żabka A, Gocek-Szczurtek N, Wróblewski M … Polit JT.
Cell biology and organellesGrowthInternational journal of molecular sciences · 2026-11-07
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, H2O2, hydrogen peroxide, nucleus, root, roots, meristem*
abstract

Replication stress (RS) is a process characterized by impaired DNA replication, resulting in the slowing down or arrest of replication forks (RFs) and in the activation of the DNA damage response. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of 24, 48, 72 and 96 h exposures of Allium cepa root meristematic cells to hydroxyurea (HU) at concentrations of 1, 2, 3 and 4 mM on cell nucleus morphology, DNA replication dynamics, mitotic activity and the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), including hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and superoxide anion (O2∙-). Furthermore, to assess epigenetic changes associated with DNA damage, the level of acetylation of lysine 56 of histone H3 (H3K56Ac) was analyzed. It was demonstrated that incubation of roots in 1 mM HU leads to the appearance of so-called interphase-mitotic (I-M) cells. Furthermore, as the HU concentration increased, inhibition of mitotic activity, a slowing down or partial inhibition of DNA replication, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) were observed. Furthermore, after 24 and 48 h of incubation with 1, 2 and 3 mM HU, a similar increase in the mean fluorescence intensity of H3K56Ac was observed, with the highest intensity recorded following treatment with 4 mM HU. Prolongation of the incubation time with the inhibitor to 72 and 96 h led to a further increase in fluorescence in the cell nuclei. The obtained results indicate that the increase in H3K56Ac levels may be associated with the accumulation of DNA damage under conditions of prolonged exposure to HU.

11.0 Arabidopsis TRB Proteins Promote ROS Detoxification for Ethanol-Enhanced Salt Stress Tolerance.
Urushihara K, Matsui A, Tanaka M … Sako K.
Abiotic stressGrowthJournal of experimental botany · 2026-11-13
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, salt stress, salinity, seed*
abstract

Soil salinization is a major threat to global agricultural productivity. Developing strategies to alleviate the effects of soil salinization is essential for maintaining stable and sustainable food production under climate change conditions. We previously showed that ethanol enhances Arabidopsis salt stress tolerance by promoting reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification through ASCORBATE PEROXIDASE (AtAPX1/2) activation. However, ethanol induces the expression of many genes beyond AtAPX1/2. Moreover, the transcriptional mechanisms underlying ethanol-mediated stress tolerance remain unclear. In this study, we identified TELOMERE REPEAT BINDING (TRB) proteins as regulators of ethanol-enhanced salt stress tolerance. Transcriptome and qRT-PCR analyses showed that TRBs regulate the expression of AtCSD1, AtCSD2, and AtCCS, which encode Cu/ZnSODs and a copper chaperone. Ethanol increased Cu/ZnSOD activity, whereas csd1 and ccs mutants were sensitive to salt stress and accumulated superoxide, even after ethanol treatment. Thus, Cu/ZnSOD-mediated detoxification contributes to ethanol-induced stress tolerance. ChIP assays showed that AtTRB3 associates with AtCSD1, AtCSD2, and AtCCS, and that ethanol treatment enhanced H4K5 acetylation at these loci. Ethanol also increased global H4 acetylation levels, suggesting that ethanol metabolism may contribute to histone acetylation. Accordingly, AtTRB proteins likely promote Cu/ZnSOD-dependent ROS detoxification through chromatin-associated gene activation, thereby contributing to ethanol-mediated salinity tolerance in Arabidopsis seedlings.

11.0 Inhibition of ROS-induced MiIDA1 and MiIDA2 gene expression by sodium hydrosulfide mitigates mango fruitlet abscission.
Kumar P, Rai AC, Keinan E, Irihimovitch V.
Kinases and signal transductionHormonesJournal of plant physiology · 2026-11-03
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, hydrogen peroxide, signaling, auxin*, IAA, ethylene
abstract

Fruitlet abscission in mango (Mangifera indica L.) is associated with enhanced ethylene perception in the abscission zone (AZ), reduced indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) transport, and increased expression of two INFLORESCENCE DEFICIENT IN ABSCISSION (MiIDA) genes. Furthermore, although reactive oxygen species (ROS) are recognized as important regulators of abscission, their specific role in mango fruitlet drop remains unclear. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) has recently emerged as a signaling molecule and antioxidant that suppresses ROS, enhancing stress tolerance while delaying senescence and inhibiting floral organ abscission in tomato. Here, we investigated the role of ROS in mango fruitlet abscission and evaluated the potential of sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS), an H2S donor, to mitigate fruitlet shedding. Using mango fruitlet-bearing explants, we monitored ROS dynamics in the AZ and their relationship with MiIDAs expression. Ethephon-induced abscission was associated with rapid ROS burst, upregulation of ROS-producing genes, and subsequent induction of MiIDA1 and MiIDA2. Similarly, exogenous hydrogen peroxide enhanced MiIDA transcripts expression and accelerated abscission. In contrast, NaHS pre-treatment significantly reduced ethephon-induced abscission and ROS accumulation in the AZ, accompanied by suppression of ROS-related genes and decreased MiIDA transcripts expression. Notably, NaHS also attenuated the induction of ethylene signaling-related genes, while not preventing the downregulation of auxin-related genes. Together, our findings suggest that NaHS mitigates mango fruitlet abscission primarily by modulating ethylene signaling, limiting ROS accumulation and repressing MiIDA genes induction. This study provides new insight into the role of ROS in abscission regulation and suggests a potential strategy for reducing fruitlet drop in mango orchards.

11.0 Investigation of the Physiological and Biochemical Effects of Brassinosteroid and Nitric Oxide in Two Wheat Varieties with Different Drought Tolerance.
Günay E, Acar O.
Kinases and signal transductionHormonesAbiotic stressPlants (Basel, Switzerland) · 2026-10-26
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, signal transduction, brassinosteroid*, osmotic stress, drought, root, seed*, development
abstract

Drought, which causes oxidative stress by increasing the amount of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plants, leads to a decrease in yield in bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.). On the other hand, nitric oxide (NO) and brassinosteroids (BRs) are known to maintain cellular homeostasis under drought stress in wheat through various signal transduction pathways. This research focuses on the individual and combined effects of NO (Sodium nitroprusside, SNP) and BR (Epibrassinolide, EBL) on physiological and biochemical parameters in two wheat varieties with different drought tolerances: under polyethylene glycol (PEG)-induced and water-scarcity-induced drought stress. Drought stress decreased ascorbate peroxidase (APX), glutathione reductase (GR), and peroxidase (POX) activities in the drought-sensitive Kenanbey variety, while increasing superoxide dismutase (SOD), GR, APX, and CAT activities in the tolerant NKÜ Lider variety. Exogenous SNP and EBL treatments effectively mitigated drought-induced membrane damage and oxidative stress, leading to significant reductions in electrolyte leakage (EL), lipid peroxidation (TBARS), and ROS accumulation in both varieties. In the NKÜ Lider, under both PEG-induced osmotic stress and water-scarcity conditions, the combined SNP and EBL treatment increased root length (RL), biomass, dry weight (DW), and SOD isoenzyme band intensity, while reducing electrolyte leakage (EL), compared with the individual treatments. In the Kenanbey variety, under water-scarcity conditions, the combined treatment improved biomass, SPAD values, CAT and POX activities, and SOD isoenzyme band intensity, while reducing EL. Additionally, the dramatically reduced SPAD and water content in both drought treatments were increased to control plant levels with individual and combined treatments of SNP and EBL. These findings highlight the potential of NO and BR treatments as promising strategies to improve physiological and biochemical responses associated with drought tolerance in wheat varieties. These findings provide experimental evidence for the development of foliar regulators for drought tolerance in wheat seedlings.

11.0 The MxMPK4-1-MxME3-7 Module Enhances ROS-Mediated Iron Deficiency Responses via Malate Metabolism in Apple.
Pi Y, Zhai L, Guo L … Wang Y.
Kinases and signal transductionAbiotic stressGrowthPlant physiology · 2026-11-13
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, kinase*, MAPK*, phosphoryl*, signaling, stress respon*, growth
abstract

Iron is an essential micronutrient required for plant growth. However, its limited bioavailability in soils often triggers Fe-deficiency stress in plants, which induces complex adaptive responses, including signaling activation and metabolic adjustment. MAPK cascade and malate metabolism are both associated with reactive oxygen species signaling. Nevertheless, their interrelationship in the plant Fe-deficiency response remains unclear. Here, metabolomic analysis revealed that the malate metabolic pathway is significantly more active in the Fe-efficient apple rootstock Malus xiaojinensis than in the Fe-inefficient rootstock Malus baccata. We identified MxME3-7, a NADP-malic enzyme, as a responsive factor to Fe deficiency stress that positively regulates Fe uptake in apple rootstocks. Additionally, MxME3-7 physically interacts with and is phosphorylated by MxMPK4-1, a kinase previously characterized as a positive modulator of the Fe-deficiency response. Notably, phosphorylation at the S201 residue of MxME3-7 significantly enhanced ROS signaling levels, thereby improving plant adaptation to Fe deficiency stress. This study elucidates the molecular mechanism of the MxMPK4-1-MxME3-7 module in ROS-mediated plant responses to Fe deficiency. These findings not only provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying plant nutritional stress responses but also offer a potential theoretical basis and genetic resources for enhancing crop tolerance to Fe deficiency stress.

10.5 Harnessing plant redox networks and bacterial modulation for next-generation abiotic stress resilience in crops.
Sarkar RK, Bhattacharyya A, Sarkar S … Mitra D.
reviewKinases and signal transductionHormonesAbiotic stressPlant physiology and biochemistry : PPB · 2026-11-07
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, signaling, phytohormone*, salinity, drought, heavy metal*, growth, development
abstract

Abiotic stresses such as drought, salinity, heavy metals, heat, and cold disrupt cellular redox homeostasis, resulting in the excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative damage that negatively affect plant growth and productivity. Under controlled conditions, lower level of ROS act as signaling molecule, whereas, at elevated levels with biotic and abiotic stress factors, causes cellular damage. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms involved in redox homeostasis in plants, including both enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant systems. The integrated roles of phytohormone signaling and plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB) in regulating ROS metabolism, boosting antioxidant capacity, and enhancing abiotic stress tolerance are further discussed. Mechanistic insights into plant stress adaptation are provided by evaluating recent advances in transcriptional regulation, epigenetic modification, and redox-associated regulatory networks. Moreover, we review the contributions of multi-omics approaches toward understanding redox regulation and identifying key molecular components involved in stress resilience. Finally, emerging applications of synthetic biology and artificial intelligence are explored as potential tools for engineering redox regulatory networks to accelerate the development of climate-resilient crops. Overall, this review provides an integrated mechanistic framework outlining how redox biology, PGPB interactions, and next-generation engineering strategies can be combined to enhance crop resilience and sustainable agricultural productivity under future environmental shifts.

10.0 Integrated Multi-Omics Analysis of the Response of Lycium barbarum 'Ningqi-1' to Powdery Mildew Infection and Functional Characterization of LbMLO6.
Xu W, Luo L, Wang J … Dai G.
Kinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunityInternational journal of molecular sciences · 2026-10-22
matched: Ca2+, reactive oxygen species, MAPK*, signal transduction, signaling, hormone*, pathogen*, defense, development, CRISPR
abstract

Powdery mildew severely constrains the production of Lycium barbarum L., yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its response to infection remain poorly understood. Here, 'Ningqi-1' plants were inoculated with the powdery mildew pathogen and sampled at 0, 12, 24, and 48 hpi for integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic analyses. Quantitative PCR and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing were further used to evaluate the candidate susceptibility gene LbMLO6. Infection induced extensive molecular reprogramming, yielding 1299 differentially expressed genes with sustained changes, 75 DAPs shared across all three time points, and 127 shared differentially accumulated metabolites. These molecules were mainly enriched in plant-pathogen interaction, plant hormone signal transduction, MAPK signaling, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and α-linolenic acid metabolism pathways, suggesting coordinated roles for Ca2+ signaling, reactive oxygen species, defense-related proteins, and secondary metabolism in the host response. Integrated multi-omics analysis identified LbMLO6 as a candidate gene associated with powdery mildew susceptibility, its expression was markedly induced from 24 hpi onward. CRISPR/Cas9-edited LbMLO6 lines showed reduced fungal development compared with the control, particularly during the early stages of infection. These findings provide preliminary evidence that LbMLO6 may be associated with powdery mildew susceptibility in L. barbarum.

10.0 Molecular Cloning, Expression Profiles, Characterization and Function of a Novel Small Heat Shock Protein (HbsHSP23.8a) in Hevea brasiliensis.
Guo H, Chen J, Yin H … Li D.
HormonesAbiotic stressGrowthPlants (Basel, Switzerland) · 2026-10-26
matched: H2O2, hydrogen peroxide, jasmon*, MeJA, hormone*, salt stress, leaf, leaves, growth, development, tree
abstract

Small heat shock proteins (sHSPs) are involved in a wide range of abiotic stresses, yet the functional roles of sHSP family genes in rubber tree salt tolerance remain largely uncharacterized. In this study, HbsHSP23.8a, a novel sHSP gene from rubber tree, was cloned and analyzed in detail. HbsHSP23.8a consists of a targeting peptide, an N-terminal domain, an α-crystallin domain (ACD), and C-terminal extensions. Additionally, putative dimer interface and conserved amino acid sequences were identified in the ACD and N-terminal domain of HbsHSP23.8a, respectively. HbsHSP23.8a transcripts were detected in different tissues and developmental stages of leaves, indicating that HbsHSP23.8a was associated with rubber tree growth and development. Besides tapping panel dryness (TPD), HbsHSP23.8a was also involved in low-temperature, high-salt, methyl jasmonate (MeJA), and ethephon (ET) responses. Under salt stress, overexpression of HbsHSP23.8a in transgenic tobacco plants exhibited greater plant height and fresh weight than wild-type (WT) plants. In addition, tobacco plants overexpressing HbsHSP23.8a increased the activities of antioxidant enzymes and decreased hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) accumulation and chlorophyll degradation under salt stress compared with the WT plants. Collectively, our results suggest that HbsHSP23.8a is related to rubber tree growth, TPD, leaf development, stress and hormone responses. Furthermore, heterologous expression of HbsHSP23.8a is associated with enhanced salt tolerance in transgenic tobacco, which may be attributed to elevated antioxidant enzyme activities, reduced cellular H2O2 accumulation, and alleviated chlorophyll degradation.

9.5 Identification of the sunflower EDL gene family reveals that HaEDL2 confers salt tolerance in sunflower.
Liu Y, Liu W, Xie Q … Chen T.
Kinases and signal transductionAbiotic stressCell biology and organellesTAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik · 2026-11-10
matched: ROS, H2O2, salt sens*, ubiquitin*, salt stress, stress respon*, nucleus
abstract

Sunflower is a globally important oilseed crop with marked stress resistance. However, the key stress-responsive genes and underlying molecular mechanisms in sunflowers remain unclear. In this study, we identified a novel salt-stress-responsive gene in sunflower, HaEDL2. The HaEDL2 protein contains conserved F-box and ELP domains and localizes to the nucleus. The HaEDL2 expression was rapidly and strongly induced under salt stress. To investigate the role of HaEDL2 in response to salt stress, we generated HaEDL2-silenced lines and subjected them to salt stress. The silenced lines exhibited significantly salt-sensitive phenotypes, with lower proline content and higher levels of MDA, H2O2, O2.- and ROS. Molecular experiments confirmed that HaEDL2 interacts with HaSKP1 and HaSKP2 and induces the expression of RAB18, RD29B, and SOS2 to be involved in salt response. Finally, haplotype analysis revealed two main HaEDL2 haplotypes that showed a strong association with the ratio of water content index. In summary, this study systematically characterized the HaEDL family and established that HaEDL2 plays a significant role in salt tolerance, providing a theoretical foundation for future research on abiotic stress in sunflowers. KEY MESSAGE : HaEDL2 encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase that confers salt tolerance in sunflower, and interacts with the SCF complex component SKP1.

9.5 Northern Light Reviews - Photosynthesis-Driven Redox Regulation Modulating ROS Levels and Physiological Responses.
Krieger-Liszkay A, Calzadilla PI.
reviewKinases and signal transductionAbiotic stressCell biology and organellesPhysiologia plantarum · 2026-11-01
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, signalling, stress respon*, nucleus, chloroplast*, development
abstract

Photosynthesis is the process through which photosynthetic organisms transform sunlight into organic carbon compounds. Beyond its role as a central metabolic pathway, photosynthetic electron transport can act as a sensitive environmental sensor. The photosynthetic apparatus maintains a complex redox homeostasis, balancing the energy absorbed from the sun with its utilization for carbon assimilation and biomass production. When the light intensity exceeds the capacity of photosynthesis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced, leading to ROS-mediated photodamage while simultaneously activating redox-driven signalling pathways. Metabolism, development and stress responses are regulated by photosynthesis-derived ROS or redox modification of target proteins, and in some cases, these molecules can trigger chloroplast-to-nucleus communication through a process known as retrograde signalling. Although a subject of many studies, the identity and relative contribution of the components involved in retrograde signalling remain largely unresolved, and the identification of the participants of such signalling pathways remains technically challenging. In this review, we will revisit the key redox regulatory pathways modulating ROS production in the photosynthetic electron transport chain. We will discuss how these pathways modulate photosynthesis and, more broadly, plant responses to the environment, and we will address shortly photosynthetic-derived ROS as signalling molecules in plant biology. Finally, we will assess the progress and remaining challenges in achieving an integrated understanding of photosynthetic redox signalling.

9.0 Comparative transcriptome analysis reveals candidate genes and defence pathways associated with resistance to potato cyst nematodes in potato (Solanum tuberosum).
Sood S, Dipta B, Bairwa A … Singh B.
Kinases and signal transductionHormonesPlant-microbe interactions and immunityFunctional plant biology : FPB · 2026-11-01
matched: calcium, calcium signal*, signalling, hormone*, immun*, pathogen*, defence, stress respon*, cell wall*, development
abstract

Globodera rostochiensis and Globodera pallida are two nematode species responsible for are potato cyst nematode (PCN) that significantly reduce potato (Solanum tuberosum) productivity worldwide. To elucidate the molecular basis of PCN resistance, we compared transcriptomic responses of the highly resistant potato breeding clone SM/11-120 with the susceptible cultivar Kufri Jyoti following simultaneous infection with both PCN species. Nematode penetration assays showed that SM/11-120 completely restricted nematode invasion up to 7 days post-inoculation (dpi), whereas Kufri Jyoti was susceptible to nematode penetration within 24 h post-inoculation (hpi) and supported juvenile development at 72 hpi and 7 dpi. RNA-sequencing (RNA-Seq) generated 18-27 million high-quality paired-end reads per library, of which 51.6-68.3% mapped uniquely to the potato reference genome. Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 724, 795, 694, and 899 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between SM/11-120 and Kufri Jyoti at 0 hpi, 24 hpi, 72 hpi, and 7 dpi, respectively. The resistant genotype exhibited enhanced expression of genes involved in immune signalling (NRC1, NBS-LRR), transcriptional regulation (WRKY, MYB), calcium signalling, pathogenesis-related proteins (PR1), hormone and defence metabolism (ACO1, geraniol 10-hydroxylase), and cell wall reinforcement (HRGP, XTH3, pectinesterase, β-expansin). Gene Ontology analysis revealed stronger enrichment of stress response, biological regulation, nitrogen compound metabolism, and response to biotic stimulus in SM/11-120 than in Kufri Jyoti. Expression patterns of selected defence-related genes were validated by quantitative reverse transcription (qRT)-PCR, confirming their rapid and sustained induction in the resistant genotype.

9.0 Heat Shock Transcription Factor B1 Coordinates Distinct bHLH Modules to Orchestrate Land Plant Adaptation
Tien, H.-C., Lin … T.-Y.
preprintKinases and signal transductionHormonesAbiotic stressbioRxiv · 2026-11-12
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, signaling, cytokinin*, heat stress, nucleus, development, morphogen*
abstract

Adaptation to terrestrial environments required the evolution of morphological structures, such as rhizoids and air pores, and robust tolerance mechanisms to environmental stress. While these innovations are well-described, the regulatory logic coordinating development with stress signaling during this transition remains largely unknown. Here, we identify Heat Shock Transcription Factor B1 (HSFB1) as a central evolutionary node that bridges this gap in Marchantia polymorpha . Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and gene regulatory network analysis, we reveal that MpHSFB1 is required to activate cell-type-specific programs for terrestrial adaptation, functioning via the regulation of cytokinin and reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis. We find that MpHSFB1 functions through a modular logic: it co-opts a specific set of bHLH transcription factors (including MpbHLH21/40) to drive developmental morphogenesis, while recruiting a distinct partner (MpbHLH51) to confer resistance to prolonged heat stress. This functional uncoupling allows a single ancestral regulator to manage disparate physiological needs. By reconstructing HSFB1 regulons across diverse plant lineages, we propose that MpHSFB1 acted as an ancestral pleiotropic hub that was effectively rewired and subfunctionalized in later angiosperm lineages for land plant evolution.

9.0 Structural studies of mitochondrial calcium uptake protein from Arabidopsis thaliana.
Yang J, Jin M, Park J … Eom SH.
Cell biology and organellesInternational journal of biological macromolecules · 2026-11-03
matched: calcium, Ca2+, mitochondri*
abstract

The mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) mediates Ca2+ uptake into the mitochondrial matrix and plays critical roles in diverse mitochondrial functions. In metazoans, MCU activity is controlled by regulatory mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake proteins (MICU) together with EMRE. Most land plants, however, lack a recognizable EMRE homolog and therefore must regulate the uniporter through a different mechanism, though no structural information has been available for any plant MICU. Arabidopsis thaliana is a model plant in which the functions of AtMCU and AtMICU have been extensively studied. Here, we report the crystal structure of Ca2+-bound AtMICU at 2.1 Å resolution. Our structure reveals that all three EF-hand motifs of AtMICU coordinate Ca2+ and that AtMICU forms a unique dimer interface characterized by a specific helix topology. Notably, Ca2+-bound AtMICU forms a novel tetrameric architecture mediated by interactions between its N-terminal helices. Our analyses further suggest that Ca2+ binding induces a conformational change in AtMICU that may facilitate a transition from a dimeric to a tetrameric state for stabilization. These findings provide a structural framework for understanding how plant MICU regulates the MCU complex in the absence of EMRE and offer insight into the evolutionarily conserved functions of MICU proteins.

8.5 HDAC1/2 mediates the chloroplast unfolded protein response through histone H4 deacetylation in Chlamydomonas.
Pan J, Xing J, Zhang C … Yang W.
Kinases and signal transductionAbiotic stressCell biology and organellesThe Plant cell · 2026-11-12
matched: ROS, H2O2, signaling, stress respon*, endoplasmic reticulum, nuclear, chloroplast*, growth
abstract

Disruption of chloroplast proteostasis activates retrograde signaling that reprograms nuclear gene expression. However, how these signals are integrated with chromatin-based transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. Here, using a genetic suppressor screen of a conditional ClpP1-depletion mutant, we identified a histone deacetylase HDAC1/2 as a regulator of chloroplast stress signaling in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Loss of HDAC1/2 alleviated growth inhibition and reduced cell death caused by disruption of chloroplast proteostasis following ClpP1 depletion. Furthermore, HDAC1/2 deficiency enhanced tolerance to high-light, oxidative, and endoplasmic reticulum stresses, as well as chloroplast translation inhibition. These stress conditions increased H2O2 levels and HDAC1/2 protein accumulation, suggesting that H2O2 may act as a common upstream signal. Additionally, HDAC1/2 deficiency also disrupted the transcriptional response to ClpP1 depletion, particularly affecting genes involved in photosynthesis, redox homeostasis, DNA metabolism, cell-cycle regulation, and ROS scavenging. This altered response was accompanied by increased histone H4 acetylation. Together, our findings identify HDAC1/2 as an important regulator connecting organellar proteostasis signaling with nuclear epigenetic regulation and suggest a role for H2O2 associated chromatin remodeling in coordinating cellular stress responses.

8.5 Integrated Physiological, Transcriptomic, and Metabolomic Analyses Reveal Coordinated Responses of the Invasive Plant Pistia stratiotes to Copper Oxide Nanoparticles.
Zhu Y, Ji WK, Xin JP … Tian RN.
HormonesCell biology and organellesGrowthPlants (Basel, Switzerland) · 2026-10-23
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, ABA, hormone*, cell wall*, root, leaf, leaves, growth
abstract

To characterize the responses of Pistia stratiotes to copper oxide nanoparticles (CuO NPs), plants were exposed to CuO NPs at nominal Cu concentrations of 0 (CK), 0.1 (T1), 1.0 (T2), 5.0 (T3), and 15.0 (T4) mg·L-1. Cu accumulation and translocation, growth, photosynthetic performance, reactive oxygen species (ROS), antioxidant responses, and molecular profiles were assessed. CuO NP exposure increased root Cu accumulation and reduced Cu translocation to leaves. Relative to CK, the bioconcentration factor (BCF) increased by 301.93% at T1 but decreased by 61.65% and 73.69% at T3 and T4, respectively. At T1, leaf chlorophyll and carotenoid contents increased, while photosynthetic performance and most chlorophyll fluorescence parameters remained largely unchanged. Nevertheless, root dry weight, relative growth rate, and stress tolerance index declined. At T3 and T4, net photosynthetic rate (Pn) decreased by 42.62-60.88% and 52.21-60.86%, respectively, accompanied by increased superoxide (O2·-) levels. Antioxidant enzyme activities also responded to exposure, while glutathione (GSH) and cysteine (Cys) contents increased at higher concentrations. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses of leaves after 14 d were conducted for CK, T1, and T3. The CK-vs.-T1 and CK-vs.-T3 comparisons identified 588 and 1088 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 166 and 352 differentially accumulated metabolites (DAMs), respectively. Comparison of transcriptomic and metabolomic results suggested associations with pectin-related cell wall processes, carotenoid biosynthesis, and hormone-related metabolism, including changes in the expression of NCED1 and other related genes, as well as in ABA-associated metabolites. Overall, the results reveal contrasting physiological responses to low and higher CuO NPs expose concentrations and identify cell wall-, carotenoid-, and hormone-related pathways for further functional investigation.

abstract

Acid mine drainage (AMD) is a pervasive global environmental challenge, and algal-based bioremediation represents one of the most robust strategies for its treatment. However, the mechanisms by which algae survive in metal-rich AMD remain largely unclear. Light is a crucial factor in plant growth, development, and productivity. While light primarily serves as the energy source to drive photosynthesis, environmental light fluctuations like vegetative shade and high-light intensity also function as signaling cues that regulate plant morphology, physiology and development. Under vegetative shade, the depletion of red and blue wavelengths reduces photosynthetic rate and triggers light signaling pathways that cause shade avoidance response (SAR). SAR promotes elongation growth and reduces photosynthetic pigment content, thereby compromising overall photosynthetic efficiency. In contrast, high-light stress occurs when light exposure exceeds the capacity of the photosynthetic apparatus, resulting in chlorophyll overexcitation, excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and subsequent oxidative damage and photoinhibition. To mitigate high-light stress, plants have developed diverse photoprotective mechanisms such as leaf and chloroplast movements, non-photochemical quenching of overexcited chlorophylls, ROS scavenging, and ATP/NADPH homeostasis. This review summarizes the molecular and physiological responses of plants to shade and high-light stress, with a particular focus on their impacts on photosynthesis. We further discuss current approaches for managing light stresses and optimizing photosynthetic performance in agriculture.

VOC perception can activate rapid signalling events, including Ca2+ influx and reactive oxygen species production; however, direct mechanistic links between these early responses and subsequent chromatin changes remain unresolved. Changes in promoter DNA methylation and histone acetylation are associated with, and in some systems functionally contribute to, regulation of VOC biosynthesis or defence responses, whereas ncRNA- and m6A-dependent mechanisms provide distinct RNA-level regulatory layers. Across diverse plant systems, chromatin states can influence VOC biosynthesis and emission, whereas in a smaller set of exposure studies, volatile cues are accompanied by changes in DNA methylation or histone modifications. Persistent or primed responses have been reported in several systems, but persistence of a phenotype or chromatin mark alone does not establish stress memory, and causal epigenetic involvement in VOC-induced memory remains unresolved. Important knowledge gaps concern the mechanisms linking volatile perception with chromatin regulation, the integration of complex VOC blends, and the relevance of these processes under field conditions. Emerging approaches, including locus-specific CRISPR/dCas-based epigenome editing and temporally resolved multi-omics, should help distinguish causal chromatin mechanisms from downstream transcriptional responses. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global threat to humankind, affecting food safety, health, and the economy. Moreover, it is evolving rapidly, resulting from the misuse and overuse of antibiotics in healthcare and agriculture a result which has emerged as a One Health challenge. It alters food systems by creating threats to food safety, food security, and public health. Such resistant microorganisms have the ability to persist and spread in the food systems, animals, water, and the environment. Such microorganisms are further sustained by the production of biofilms. There is increased demand for safe and sustainable alternatives as a result of the limited applicability of conventional antibiotics and chemical preservatives. Plant-mediated phyto-nanoparticles (PNPs) are emerging antimicrobials. A PRISMA-compliant literature search and bibliometric analysis were used to identify leading research trends and gaps. This review evaluates their applicability in different aspects of food safety and preservation and in mitigating AMR. It includes major foodborne pathogens, resistance mechanisms, biofilm formation, and synthesis of bioactive nanoparticles using plants. The main antimicrobial mechanisms of these nanoparticles include the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), disruption of the cell membrane, release of metal ions, enzyme inhibition, DNA damage, and interference with quorum sensing. This review includes their applicability in active food packaging, edible coatings, food preservation, and food processing surfaces. This review expands existing research by including the results of real food matrices and storage studies. The review incorporates the emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in nanoparticles design, prediction of antimicrobial activities, and optimization of synthesis parameters, and trend identification. In general, PNPs have a lot of potential for sustainable approaches to food preservation. However, standardized methods, rigorous safety evaluation, AI/ML-assisted optimization, and real-food, in vivo, and industrial studies are needed for successful translation.

Verticillium wilt severely limits global cotton production, yet the molecular basis of early resistance in upland cotton remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated time-series transcriptomics and untargeted metabolomics to resolve early defense dynamics in cotton seedling roots of the VW-resistant cultivar Jinken1775 and the susceptible cultivar Junmian1 at 0, 4, 8, 12, 24, and 72 h post-inoculation (hpi) with Verticillium dahliae. Results revealed distinct early defense dynamics. The resistant genotype exhibited restrained yet sustained transcriptional activation coupled with preferential flavonoid/lipid accumulation, whereas the susceptible cultivar displayed disordered reprogramming. Integrated analysis of DEGs and DAMs resolved resistance circuits enriched in calcium signaling, membrane remodeling, and secondary metabolism. Network inference positioned GhWRKY33 as a central hub connecting early signal transduction with downstream metabolic reprogramming. Virus-induced gene silencing of GhWRKY33 significantly compromised cotton resistance to V. dahliae, indicating its positive regulatory role in the defense response. Haplotype analysis across 419 upland cotton accessions further revealed that favorable GhWRKY33 alleles are preferentially enriched in resistant lines. This study provided molecular targets for genetic improvement of disease resistance.

However, the role of the RLK gene MIK2 (Male discoverer 1-Interacting receptor-like Kinase 2) in regulating cotton resistance to Verticillium dahliae remains unclear. Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of GbMIK2 or CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knocking out of GhMIK2 increased cotton resistance to V. dahliae infection, while ectopic expression of GbMIK2 in Arabidopsis thaliana decreased the plant resistance, indicating a negative role of GbMIK2 in cotton Verticillium wilt resistance. GbMIK2 interacted with its co-receptor GbBAK1 during V. dahliae infection in the initial immune response, resulting in activation of the MAPK cascade. GbMIK2 interacted in the membrane and nucleus with GbOCP3, which also plays a negative role in Verticillium wilt resistance. Both GbMIK2 and GbOCP3 are located in the membrane and nucleus. Their interaction blocked the reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst and jasmonic acid (JA)-mediated resistance to V. dahliae, resulting in suppression of cotton resistance to Verticillium wilt. These results collectively indicate that GbMIK2, interacting with GbOCP3, acts as a negative regulator in modulating cotton Verticillium wilt resistance, providing new insights to the understanding of mechanisms of RLKs in cotton disease resistance.
