Plant viral diseases cause substantial agricultural losses, yet the endogenous signals contributing to antiviral immunity remain poorly understood. In this study, we performed comparative peptidomic profiling of three tobacco cultivars with contrasting resistance to potato virus Y (PVY), namely, Coker176 with high resistance, CS01 with moderate resistance, and NC95 with high susceptibility, and identified distinct resistance-associated peptide occurrence and accumulation patterns. Among the candidate peptides derived from known signalling-peptide precursors, PSK #2 exhibited significant antiviral activity. Sequence analyses revealed that PSK #2 originates from a noncanonical region of the PSK3 precursor distinct from the conserved YIYTQ motif; therefore, it was designated a NbPSK3-derived peptide (NbPSK3-DP). Genetic analyses revealed that the NbPSK3 precursor positively regulates PVY resistance in tobacco, whereas its disruption increases shoot branching. Mechanistically, NbPSK3-DP rapidly activates MPK3/MPK6 phosphorylation and induces a transient ROS burst. Functional analyses revealed that NbSnRK2 and NbACS1 contribute to NbPSK3-mediated antiviral resistance. Phytohormone profiling revealed coordinated changes in jasmonic acid (JA)-related metabolites, and exogenous JA treatment decreased PVY accumulation in cr-nbpsk3 plants, supporting the involvement of JA-associated signalling. Additionally, both NbPSK3 overexpression and exogenous NbPSK3-DP application increased resistance to multiple tested plant viruses. Together, our findings identify a noncanonical bioactive peptide derived from the NbPSK3 precursor and demonstrate the utility of comparative peptidomics for identifying endogenous peptide regulators of antiviral immunity.

Plants, as sessile organisms, must continually adapt to fluctuating temperatures to ensure survival. The plasma membrane-localized receptor-like kinase FERONIA (FER) coordinates diverse physiological processes and responses to various biotic and abiotic stresses. However, the role of FER in plant adaptation to elevated temperatures remains largely unexplored. Here, we report that FER is indispensable for plant growth and survival at warm temperatures. We found that fer loss-of-function mutants exhibit impaired thermomorphogenic growth and are hypersensitive to mild heat stress, displaying extensive oxidative stress-mediated cell death at elevated temperatures. Combined genetic and molecular analyses revealed that these temperature-sensitive defects in fer mutants are caused by an overaccumulation of jasmonic acid (JA), which subsequently triggers excessive production of reactive oxygen species. Furthermore, we show that this aberrant JA accumulation and oxidative stress are attributable to impaired FER-mediated regulation of turgor-dependent cell wall tensile stress. Taken together, our results suggest that FER-mediated cell wall tensile stress regulation serves as a critical mechanism to prevent aberrant JA accumulation and oxidative stress at sustained elevated temperatures, thereby enabling plants to adapt to and survive under such conditions.

Abstract Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinases (MAP4Ks/MAPKKKKs) reside at the apex of MAPK signalling cascades, yet their roles in potato abiotic stress responses remain unexplored. Here, we identified eight StMAPKKKK genes via genome-wide identification in potato. StMAPKKKK1 protein was strongly induced by salt and drought stress and localized to the plasma membrane and cytoplasm. Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and split-luciferase complementation (SLC) experiments show that StMAPKKKK1 physically interacts with StMAPKK2. To assess its function, we generated StMAPKKKK1- overexpressing (OE) and RNA interference (RNAi) lines in potato cultivar 'Atlantic' . OE lines exhibited improved growth, with higher plant height, biomass, and leaf number, whereas RNAi lines were more sensitive than non-transgenic (NT) controls under both salt and drought stress conditions. Higher activities of ascorbate peroxidase (APX), catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and peroxidase (POD), as well as proline and total chlorophyll contents, along with lower levels of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) and malondialdehyde (MDA) were observed in OE lines. In contrast, RNAi lines showed opposite trends for all above-mentioned parameters. These results indicate alleviated oxidative damage, enhanced osmotic adjustment, and better pigment retention. This study presents the first functional characterization of the StMAPKKKK family in potato and establishes StMAPKKKK1 as a positive regulator of salt and drought tolerance, acting at least partially through interaction with StMAPKK2 and activation of the antioxidant defense system.

abstract

Plant receptor-like kinases (RLKs) constitute one of the largest and most ancient protein families in land plants. Localized on the plasma membrane, they perceive a diverse array of extracellular signals and coordinate intracellular responses that are crucial for plant growth, development, immunity, and adaptation to environmental changes. Over the past two decades, there has been an explosive expansion of knowledge regarding how RLKs govern virtually every aspect of plant life. Crucially, this knowledge has been translated into practical applications for crop improvement. Here, we summarize the conspicuous triumphs of RLK-mediated strategies in improving plant architecture and yield, enhancing biotic stress resistance against insect herbivores and microbial pathogens, as well as bolstering abiotic stress tolerance to heat, cold, drought, and salinity. We also discuss how RLKs have been utilized as precision molecular targets through genome editing, promoter engineering, and other biotechnological approaches, offering a roadmap for sustainable crop improvement.

Susceptibility genes in plants promote pathogen infection by supporting compatible pathogen-plant interactions. However, how plants restrict the functions of susceptibility factors to promote immunity remains largely unclear. In this study, we isolated and characterized an apple susceptibility gene MdSTK1 (the STE20 family serine/threonine-protein kinase 1) whose expression was induced by Cytospora mali infection. The overexpression of MdSTK1 significantly compromised resistance to C. mali, whereas silencing of the MdSTK1 gene enhanced resistance in apple. MdSTK1 physically interacted with the leucine-rich repeat receptor-like kinase MdRLKT23. MdRLKT23 positively regulated apple resistance to C. mali. MdRLKT23 could also phosphorylate MdSTK1. MdRLKT23 promoted an MG132-sensitive/proteasome-dependent reduction in MdSTK1 protein abundance, thereby activating plant immunity. Taken together, our study provides mechanistic insights into how an apple LRR-RLK regulates the protein stability of the susceptibility factor MdSTK1 to trigger immunity. The application of this MdRLKT23-MdSTK1 immune module will lay a foundation for resistance breeding in fruit trees.

Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) is frequently affected by drought stress during growth and development. UDP-glucose 4-epimerase (UGE) catalyzes the reversible conversion between UDP-glucose and UDP-galactose, but its function in cotton drought tolerance remains unclear. Here, the upland cotton UGE gene family was characterized, and GhUGE2 was selected for further analysis. The GhUGE2 promoter contains several stress-responsive cis-elements. Overexpression of GhUGE2 enhanced drought tolerance, reduced water loss, ROS accumulation, and lipid peroxidation, and increased antioxidant enzyme activities. Nitraria tangutorum is a pioneer shrub species for windbreak and sand fixation in desert regions. Drought stress caused by continuous global warming poses a significant environmental challenge to the growth and development of N. tangutorum. This study employed the N. tangutorum 2-17-16 from the Zhangye provenance as the experimental material to analyze the physiological and biochemical changes and transcriptome data of N. tangutorum seedlings under PEG-simulated drought stress, systematically elucidating the regulatory mechanisms underlying responses to drought stress in N. tangutorum at physiological and molecular levels. Furthermore, the function of the core regulatory gene NtPP2C51-like in drought resistance responses of N. tangutorum was investigated via heterologous overexpression in Nicotiana benthamiana. The results indicated that N. tangutorum responded to PEG-simulated drought stress by specifically increasing the content of osmoprotectants and activity of antioxidant enzymes. Under PEG-simulated drought stress, differentially expressed genes were significantly enriched in pathways such as Plant hormone signal transduction and MAPK signaling pathway-plant. Genes such as IAA, GID1, ETR, EBF1/2, and PP2C play significant roles in the response of N. tangutorum to drought stress. Under drought stress, N. benthamiana plants overexpressing NtPP2C51-like exhibited faster water loss, higher MDA content, lower contents of osmoprotectants, and lower antioxidant enzyme activities than wild-type plants. At 7 d of drought treatment, MDA content in the overexpression lines was 1.31-1.39-fold higher, whereas soluble sugar content was only 57-61% of that in wild-type plants, indicating that NtPP2C51-like overexpression increases drought sensitivity in the heterologous N. benthamiana system and suggesting a potential negative role of NtPP2C51-like in the drought response of N. tangutorum. These results provide a theoretical basis for understanding the physiological and molecular mechanisms underlying drought adaptation in N. tangutorum and provide candidate genes for further drought-tolerance studies and genetic improvement of this ecologically important desert plant overall.

abstract

Male reproductive development in plants relies on the precise patterning of anther locules and the specification of the tapetum layer. While the BRASSINAZOLE RESISTANT (BZR) family transcription factors are essential for both processes, they function independently of the brassinosteroid (BR) receptors, leaving their upstream signaling mechanism unknown. Here, through systematic genetic analysis, we show that a core BR-signaling module, comprising BR-SIGNALING KINASEs (BSKs) and BRASSINOSTEROID-INSENSITIVE 2 (BIN2), is repurposed downstream of the tapetum regulator the receptor kinase EXCESS MICROSPOROCYTES1 (EMS1) and functions upstream of BZRs. Within this reconfigured pathway, EMS1 recruits BSKs, which in turn inactivate BIN2, thereby releasing BZRs in a conserved hierarchy cascade mirroring BR signaling to drive tapetum specification. Additionally, this BSKs-BIN2-BZRs signaling module also functions in anther locule formation. Conversely, BSU1-LIKE2/3 (BSL2/3), homologs of the positive BR regulator BSU1, act as repressors in this context. This pathway transcriptionally activates the cyclins such as CYCB1;1 to initiate tapetal cell division, while BSL2/3 ensure its timely termination by promoting CYCB1;1 protein degradation. Our work defines the signaling framework governing anther development and establishes a paradigm in which conserved signaling components are rewired to achieve developmental specificity.

Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, is the most destructive fungal disease of rice, responsible for annual yield losses of 10-30% and posing a major threat to global food security. The rapid evolution of blast pathotypes and the polygenic nature of resistance complicate breeding efforts for durable resistance. In this study, we integrated multiple RNA-sequencing datasets, revealing a dynamic transcriptional landscape during infection. Compared with susceptible genotypes, resistant genotypes showed early downregulation of immune receptors (e.g., OsPtr, OsSAH2, OsWRKY64), followed by active upregulation of defense effectors (e.g., OsPR10b, chitinases, OsLsi6, OSMORF8a) during peak response stages. Key pathways, such as immune signaling, receptor kinases, and secondary metabolism, were enriched in resistance modules, whereas susceptibility was linked mainly to primary metabolism. Machine learning (ML) models, especially XGBoost (XGB), achieved high area under the curve (AUC) of up to 0.98 in predicting resistance, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis highlighting known and novel genes, including OsLP2, NB-ARC domain protein, OsRPM1, OsATG8d, and several uncharacterized proteins. Importantly, ML identified regulators that conventional methods missed, underscoring the value of integrated computational approaches. Functional validation of OsRPM1 using CRISPR/Cas9 knockout (KO) and overexpression (OX) lines confirmed its positive role in blast resistance, where KO mutants exhibited increased lesion length and higher pathogen accumulation. In contrast, OX lines showed enhanced resistance and improved photosynthetic performance and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) accumulation. These findings provide a comprehensive resource of candidate genes and regulatory modules for functional validation and molecular breeding, offering a robust foundation for developing rice cultivars with broad-spectrum and durable blast resistance.

Sclerotinia sclerotiorum is one of the most destructive soilborne plant fungal pathogens, devastating many economically important oilseed and vegetable crops. Its overwintering dormant structure sclerotia can survive in soil for years under harsh environments, making disease control particularly challenging. Despite its economic importance, the molecular understanding of sclerotia formation and virulence mechanisms remains fragmented. In this study, throughs both forward genetic screening and reverse genetic analysis, we identified and characterised key components of the cell wall integrity (CWI) MAPK cascade in S. sclerotiorum. Loss-of-function mutants of MAPKKK SsBck1, MAPKK SsMkk1, and MAPK SsSmk3, as well as the scaffold protein SsPro40, exhibited complete loss of sclerotia formation, defect in compound appressorium development, and abolished virulence. Genetic and MAPK phosphorylation analysis further revealed dual requirements of both the CWI cascade and the pheromone MAPK pathway in sclerotia development and virulence. In addition, the conserved CWI downstream transcription factor SsAdv1 was identified as a major regulator of sclerotia formation. Finally, we demonstrated that CWI kinases can serve as effective targets of host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) to suppress Sclerotinia stem rot. Collectively, our findings reveal a regulatory network involving the CWI and pheromone MAPK cascades that coordinates fungal growth, virulence, and sclerotia formation in S. sclerotiorum, providing potential molecular targets for disease control.

Manganese (Mn) homeostasis, the precise regulation of cellular Mn levels, is crucial for plant growth and is maintained primarily through the transporter NATURAL RESISTANCE-ASSOCIATED MACROPHAGE PROTEIN 1 (NRAMP1). While the kinases responsible for its phosphorylation are well-established, the phosphatases mediating its dephosphorylation remain unidentified. We identify ABI1 and ABI2 as the phosphatases acting on NRAMP1, linking ABA signaling to Mn homeostasis. Mn stresses trigger ABA to inhibit ABI1/2, which may enable NRAMP1 phosphorylation and stress initiation. A feedback loop then appears to induce short-term ABI1/2 reactivation, mediating site-specific dephosphorylation of NRAMP1 at Thr498 (to fine-tune uptake under deficiency) and at Ser20 (to limit endocytosis under toxicity). This dephosphorylation restrains overactivation and contributes to the maintenance of Mn ion balance. Subsequent ABI1/2 attenuation may facilitates long-term adaptation. Collectively, our findings support the ABA-ABI1/2-NRAMP1 axis as a feedback-regulated circuit controlling Mn homeostasis; this work reveals an expanded functional repertoire for ABA-signaling PP2Cs and identifies a targetable module for enhancing crop resilience to Mn stress.

abstract

BZR1 (Brassinazole-resistant 1) and BES1 (bri1-EMS suppressor1) are the principal transcription factors that convert brassinosteroid (BR) perception into genome-wide transcriptional programs governing plant growth, development, and stress responses. Once regarded as end-effectors of a linear receptor-to-nucleus relay, they are now recognized as central hubs that integrate diverse endogenous and environmental cues into context-specific transcriptional outputs. We synthesize recent progress across four connected levels. Structurally, a modular architecture enables simultaneous target recognition, signal input, and output control. Mechanistically, the canonical BIN2-mediated phosphorylation switch is expanded by upstream regulators that couple membrane dynamics, carbon status, protein homeostasis, and nuclear import to BZR1/BES1, while ubiquitination, SUMOylation, redox modification, and acetylation form an interconnected post-translational network. During transcriptional execution, dephosphorylated BZR1/BES1 partition targets into activated and repressed sets through cis-element preference, corepressor recruitment, chromatin modifiers, and partnerships with factors such as PIF4 and ARF6. Physiologically, BZR1/BES1 coordinate anutrient-responsive metabolism, yield-related traits, and abiotic-stress tolerance, with marked functional divergence among crop orthologs. We highlight open questions in signal-integration specificity and discuss how BZR1/BES1 modules could be engineered for climate-resilient crops.

Abstract Gliadin is a major trigger of allergic responses to wheat-based products. Although previous studies have shown that polyphenol intervention or physical modification can attenuate its immunoreactivity, the combined effects of polyphenols and high hydrostatic pressure (HHP) on this property remain poorly understood, and the optimal processing order is unclear. The energy-sensing VvSnRK1 complex, a key regulator of sugar signaling and energy homeostasis, was investigated in 'Kyoho' grape seedlings under high-temperature (HT), waterlogging (WL), and combined stress (HW). Single HT induced the most pronounced malondialdehyde and proline peaks. These stresses upregulated VvSnRK1α/β/γ gene expression and protein levels, along with increased VvSnRK1α phosphorylation. Functional analysis revealed that the phosphomimetic mutant TD enhanced protein stability and extended kinase activity to 16 h, while the non-phosphorylatable TA mutant lost function due to accelerated ubiquitination-mediated degradation. 23.0 Phytohormonal crosstalk: a plant defense network in response to abiotic and biotic stresses.
Alhammad BA, Seleiman MF.
reviewCa2+Kinases and signal transductionPlant-microbe interactions and immunityFrontiers in plant science · 2026-10-30
matched: ROS, reactive oxygen species, signal transduction, signaling, auxin*, abscisic acid, ABA, gibberellin*, cytokinin*, ethylene, jasmon*, JA
abstract

Plants are continuously subjected to a variety of environmental stresses, including biotic (such as herbivores and pathogens) and abiotic (such as drought, salinity, heat and cold stresses). Their ability to survive under such adverse conditions relies on highly coordinated and sophisticated phytohormonal signaling networks. Major plant hormones including abscisic acid (ABA), ethylene (ET), salicylic acid (SA), auxins, jasmonic acid (JA), gibberellins (GAs) and cytokinins (CKs) are involved in stress perception, defense mechanisms, growth, and development of plants. These hormones modulate gene expression, activate signal transduction cascades, regulate metabolic pathways and control key physiological processes such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification, osmoprotectant accumulation and stomatal movement. Evidence is accumulating that hormonal signaling pathways extensively cross-talk, enabling plants to balance growth and stress responses under unfavorable conditions. Moreover, phytohormone-mediated regulatory mechanisms are closely related with epigenetic modifications, RNA-based regulation and transcription factor networks that are involved in stress memory and priming, enabling plants to respond more quickly and efficiently to repeated stress events. This review summarizes the current knowledge of the roles of phytohormones in plant stress responses, especially their molecular mechanisms, signaling integration and hormonal interactions. Despite substantial progress, major knowledge gaps remain in understanding how interconnected hormonal networks integrate with transcriptional, epigenetic, metabolic, and redox processes, particularly under combined, fluctuating, and recurrent stresses. Future research integrating multi-omics, advanced phenotyping, systems biology, and precision breeding will be essential for resolving these context-dependent regulatory networks and translating mechanistic insights into high-yielding, climate-resilient crops.

18.0 Phytohormonal regulation of plant immunity under biotic stress: Mechanisms, crosstalk, and sustainable management strategies.
Younas MU, Jamali ZH, Qasim M … Gururani MA.
reviewCa2+Kinases and signal transductionPlant-microbe interactions and immunityPlant physiology and biochemistry : PPB · 2026-11-02
matched: reactive oxygen species, receptor*, peptide hormone*, auxin*, abscisic acid, gibberellin*, cytokinin*, ethylene, jasmon*, salicylic acid, brassinosteroid*, strigolactone*
abstract

Biotic stress caused by pathogens and herbivores remains a major constraint on crop productivity. Plant immunity is regulated by an interconnected hormonal network in which salicylic acid, jasmonic acid, and ethylene interact with abscisic acid, auxin, cytokinins, gibberellins, brassinosteroids, strigolactones, and peptide hormones. This review synthesizes evidence on hormonal control of receptor-mediated immunity, reactive oxygen species, secondary metabolism, pathogen manipulation, and growth-defense trade-offs. Three conclusions emerge. First, hormonal effects are conditional on pathogen lifestyle, infection stage, tissue, dosage, genotype, and environment; therefore, individual hormones cannot be assigned universally protective or susceptibility-promoting roles. Second, pathogens exploit hormonal crosstalk, while constitutive defense activation can reduce growth, fertility, yield, or abiotic-stress tolerance. Third, omics, biosensors, spatial profiling, and genome editing can identify regulatory nodes, but their agricultural value depends on causal validation and field performance. We propose phytohormonal immune architecture as a framework for integrating these processes. Effective deployment should prioritize inducible, tissue-specific, and dose-controlled regulation through priming, beneficial microbes, breeding, promoter engineering, and targeted delivery. Hormone-based strategies should complement established crop-protection practices and be evaluated jointly for pathogen restriction, productivity, environmental stability, and physiological cost.

Abstract The application of the established somatic embryogenesis (SE) system of Korean pine ( Pinus koraiensis ) has been largely limited by strong genotype dependence in embryogenic callus (EC) induction. To identify genotype-dependent markers for screening responsive genotypes, we compared physiological traits of one sensitive Korean pine EC-producing genotype and two recalcitrant genotypes: one that produces low-embryogenic callus (LEC) and another that produces non-embryogenic callus (NEC). At the early stage of embryogenic competence acquisition, the EC genotype was characterized by higher indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), methyl jasmonate (MeJA), peroxidase (POD), and malondialdehyde (MDA), coupled with moderate hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ), while exhibiting lower abscisic acid (ABA) and catalase (CAT). In contrast, the LEC genotype had lower ZR but higher IAA/ABA, MeJA/ABA, gibberellins (GA 3 )/ABA, brassinosteroids (BR)/ABA, and ZR/ABA ratios, with significantly reduced SOD, potentially explaining its late‑stage loss of embryogenic competence. Pinus massoniana Lamb. is an important timber- and oleoresin-producing tree species in southern China. Copalyl diphosphate synthase (CPS) catalyzes the cyclization of geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP) to copalyl diphosphate (CPP), representing a key step in the biosynthesis of gibberellins (GAs) and diverse diterpenoids. 14.0 MAPK signaling in plant metabolic control: integrating phytohormones with primary and secondary metabolism.

reviewKinases and signal transductionPlant-microbe interactions and immunityAbiotic stressJournal of genetics and genomics = Yi chuan xue bao · 2026-11-12

abstract

Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades are conserved signaling modules that integrate environmental and developmental cues to regulate plant metabolism. This review synthesizes current understanding of how MAPKKK-MAPKK-MAPK cascades coordinate primary metabolism, secondary metabolism, and phytohormone biosynthesis. MAPK cascades regulate photosynthetic capacity, nitrogen fixation and assimilation, and carbon flux through phosphorylation of key metabolic enzymes and transcription factors that balance growth with stress responses. In secondary metabolism, MAPK cascades converge on downstream transcription factors to regulate camalexin, indole glucosinolate, phenylpropanoid, flavonoid, lignin, terpenoid, and alkaloid biosynthesis. We further summarize how MAPKs are involved in the biosynthesis and signaling of ethylene, jasmonic acid, salicylic acid, auxin, and abscisic acid, revealing extensive crosstalk between kinase cascades and hormonal networks. We propose an integrative model in which MAPK cascades function as signaling hubs funneling upstream cues into three coordinated arms: transcription factor phosphorylation, direct modulation of structural enzymes, and phytohormone crosstalk. Future research should address key knowledge gaps, including incomplete MAPK cascades, limited understanding of MAPK substrates and their specificity in metabolic regulation, feedback mechanisms preventing metabolic overactivation, and the conservation of these principles across crop species. Understanding MAPK-mediated metabolic control holds promise for engineering stress-resilient, pathogen-resistant, and high-yield crops.

Abstract To address issues such as the low utilization rate of tomato straw resources and prominent continuous cropping obstacles in greenhouse tomato seedling cultivation, this study used autogenous tomato straw-derived pyrolysis liquid (TSPL) as the material, with distilled water as a control (CK). 13.0 Phytoliths as Structural, Physiological Integrators of Multifunctional Defense and Climate Resilience in Grasses.
Bhat MA, Charak N, Singh H … Hakeem KR.
reviewCa2+Kinases and signal transductionPlant-microbe interactions and immunityBiology · 2026-11-04

abstract

Grasses (Poaceae) are the foremost silicon (Si) accumulators among terrestrial plants. Plants take up Si as monosilicic acid, Si(OH)4, which polymerizes in cells and tissues such as the epidermis, xylem and phloem to form phytogenic (biogenic) silica, SiO2 · nH2O, deposited as phytoliths. This review, based on a documented literature search with explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, evaluates evidence that phytoliths protect grasses against herbivores, fungal and bacterial pathogens and nematodes, and against drought, heat, salinity, metal toxicity, UV-B radiation and mechanical stress, and it examines combined stresses under climate change. We distinguish phytolith-specific evidence from studies that supplied soluble Si or Si nanoparticles, and we grade the evidence for each proposed mechanism. Physical mechanisms (abrasion, mechanical and apoplastic barriers, reduced non-stomatal water loss) are the best supported. Biochemical and hormonal mechanisms, including jasmonic acid, salicylic acid and ethylene signaling, remain hypotheses because Si(OH)4 is chemically inert and much of the evidence is correlative. Elevated CO2 can lower foliar Si concentration in some grasses, which may weaken protection, but effects on total Si accumulation and function are poorly known. Phytolith-occluded carbon is a potential but uncertain carbon sink. We identify research priorities and practical implications for crop, pasture and carbon management.

Alkaline salt stress is an important abiotic stress factor that restricts the growth and development of potato (Solanum tuberosum L.). It can induce oxidative damage, disrupt cellular structures, and disturb endogenous hormone homeostasis, thereby impairing normal plant growth and development. However, the physiological mechanisms underlying potato responses to alkaline salt stress, as well as the relationships among antioxidant defense, lignin accumulation, and changes in endogenous hormone levels, remain to be fully elucidated. Therefore, a systematic investigation of potato responses to alkaline salt stress at both the physiological and gene expression levels is needed to provide further insights into the underlying stress-response mechanisms. In this study, potato cultivar 'Atlantic' was used as the experimental material, and a pot experiment was conducted with four NaHCO3 concentrations: 0 mmol/L (CK), 20 mmol/L (T1), 40 mmol/L (T2), and 60 mmol/L (T3). Changes in the antioxidant system, root lignin accumulation, and endogenous hormone contents under different levels of alkaline salt stress were quantitatively analyzed. In addition, the expression patterns of genes involved in lignin biosynthesis (phenylpropanoid pathway) and ABA, GA, and BR signaling pathways were examined to establish an integrated model of the responses involving antioxidant defense, hormone regulation, and lignin biosynthesis. The results showed that the degree of oxidative stress progressively increased with increasing NaHCO3 concentration. SOD (superoxide dismutase) activity and the contents of MDA (malondialdehyde) and GSH (glutathione) continuously increased, whereas POD(peroxidase) and CAT (catalase) activities exhibited a pattern of first increasing and then decreasing, reaching their maximum levels under 40 mmol/L NaHCO3 treatment. Root lignin content increased progressively with increasing stress intensity. In addition, alkaline salt stress significantly affected endogenous hormone levels, with ABA and BR contents increasing and GA content decreasing as the NaHCO3 concentration increased. Further analysis revealed that alkaline salt stress altered the expression of genes involved in the phenylpropanoid pathway and ABA (abscisic acid), GA (gibberellin), and BR (brassinosteroid) signaling pathways, indicating coordinated responses involving antioxidant defense, lignin biosynthesis, and hormonal regulation. This study provides insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying potato responses to alkaline salt stress and provides a theoretical basis for stress-resilient potato cultivation and the breeding of salt- and alkali-tolerant cultivars in saline-alkali soils.

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is an essential staple crop worldwide, and tillering acts as a key target for molecular breeding because of its critical contribution to grain yield. In this study, a high-tillering dwarf mutant designated htd8 was isolated from an ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-mutagenized population of indica rice cultivar 'Shuangkezao (SKZ)'. The mutant exhibits reduced plant height, dramatically increased tiller number, shortened and yellow-chlorotic leaves. Drought stress (DS) impairs growth and metabolism in tea plants, and exogenous hormones are important regulators of drought responses. Brassica napus L. (rapeseed), a member of the family Brassicaceae, is the world's third most important oilseed crop for edible oil production, after soybean and palm. Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping is a powerful strategy for dissecting the genetic basis of seed weight. In this review, Previous studies summarized a total of 1905 candidate genes associated with seed weight in Brassica napus. Five candidate genomic regions harboring 204 seed-weight-related genes were identified, among which 21 genes were characterized as differentially expressed genes via transcriptomic analysis. Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) mutant libraries targeting genes related to silique and seed size have been constructed in Brassica napus, revealing that BnaHRD genes play critical roles in seed development. These differentially expressed genes are involved in developmental processes, cell division. and nutrient storage, supporting their functions in seed size regulation. SHB1 and HAIKU2 modulate endosperm proliferation through the IKU pathway, thereby affecting seed weight. BZR1 (brassinazole-resistant 1) acts as a master regulator of seed growth via maternal tissues. Thidiazuron (TDZ), a cytokinin analogue, simultaneously promotes cell proliferation and cell expansion, thereby increasing cell number and cell size. Multiple phytohormone signaling pathways, including auxin, gibberellin (GA), and brassinosteroid (BR), as well as transcription factors such as LEC2, participate in the regulatory network of seed size. Here, we review current advances in the genetic and molecular regulation of seed size and discuss future perspectives for rapeseed breeding.

Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) is a typical non-climacteric fruit whose development and ripening are coordinately regulated by auxin (IAA), abscisic acid (ABA) and sucrose signaling. However, stage-specific interactions among these signals in controlling cell expansion and anthocyanin biosynthesis remain incompletely understood. Results showed that IAA maintained compact cell arrangement, delayed tissue loosening and softening, suppressed anthocyanin accumulation and the expression of anthocyanin biosynthetic genes (FaCHS, FaCHI, FaF3H, FaDFR, FaANS, FaUFGT, etc.), and limited sugar accumulation across stages. In contrast, ABA and sucrose treatments promoted cell expansion and intercellular space enlargement (especially from WT to FR), accelerated softening by elevating polygalacturonase (PG), pectin methylesterase (PME) and cellulase activities, markedly increased anthocyanin content and CIRG values, enhanced soluble sugar accumulation, and upregulated anthocyanin pathway, sugar metabolism/transport (FaSPS1, FaSUTs) and ripening-related genes (FaNCEDs, FaSnRK2.6, etc.). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that early high IAA levels drive cell expansion while repressing ABA and ripening programs, whereas the subsequent decline of IAA and rise of ABA and sucrose coordinately trigger anthocyanin biosynthesis, sugar accumulation and softening. At 100 mM NaCl, SA provided the greatest photosynthetic protection: it maintained net CO2 assimilation (A) and increased total plant dry weight (TPDW) and pigment content compared with plants without growth regulators at the same salinity. At 200 mM NaCl, IAA increased TPDW whilst maintaining leaf growth, A, and water- and nitrogen-use efficiencies. These benefits coincided with higher ascorbate peroxidase activity, higher proline concentrations and high phenolic contents, and lower ethylene production. GA3 preserved pigments and photosynthetic activity, KIN promoted leaf growth, and SPD increased root biomass. This review systematically summarizes the multifaceted roles of key genes in the jasmonate biosynthesis and degradation pathway, such as LOXs, AOSs, AOCs, OPRs, ACXs, MFPs, KATs, JAR1, CYP94s and JOXs/JAOs, in plant growth and development, as well as in responses to biotic and abiotic stresses. We highlight that current evidence suggests that jasmonate biosynthesis and degradation are regulated through a complex network involving multiple gene families operating across different subcellular compartments. These genes are also reported to be associated with interactions between jasmonate metabolism and other signaling pathways, including light and hormones such as auxin, cytokinin, and ethylene. Finally, we identify current research gaps and propose future directions, including tissue-specific mechanisms, multi-signal integration, and applications in non-model plants.

Abstract Low-temperatures severely limit tomato seed germination, leading to reduced crop yields. Elucidating the cold resistance regulatory mechanisms is crucial for cold-resistant breeding. This study used the cold-tolerant tomato inbred line F266 and the cold-sensitive inbred line M196 as experimental materials. Phenotypic analysis revealed that under normal-temperature conditions of 25°C, there was no significant difference in germination rates between the two inbred lines. However, under low-temperature treatment of 16°C, F266 germinated earlier and exhibited a more pronounced advantage in hypocotyl elongation. Comparative transcriptome analysis results indicate that the two lines exhibit genotype-specific differences in oxidative stress response, carbohydrate metabolism, and plant hormone signaling pathways. F266 has a stronger antioxidant response capability, with higher accumulation of galactinol, raffinose, and sucrose. At the same time, F266 has higher endogenous auxin (IAA) and gibberellin (GA₃) content, and genes related to auxin and gibberellin show differential expression. 9.5 Flooding-induced hypoxic stress: implications of reactive nitrogen species for oxidative stress tolerance in plants.

Oxygen deficiency in the environment is a stress for plants, manifesting as hypoxia and anoxia. A steeper gradient of oxygen depletion from its saturated cellular concentration is observed under oxidative stress, where nitrogen intermediates play pivotal roles in the recognition and transmission of hypoxic signals. Under hypoxic conditions, the major metabolic shifts are manifested with the fermentation pathway and the development of oxidative redox, where reactive nitrogen species (RNS) have been recorded to have significant beneficial roles. This review highlights hypoxia-induced oxidative redox signaling from rhizospheric soil and stress tolerance gene induction under RNS coverage across different modalities. The biosynthetic and catabolic pathways of RNS via the nitrate-nitrite and phytoglobin cycles, highlighting the regulation of ROS scavenging and redox homeostasis against joint nitro-oxidative stress, were emphasized. At the cellular level, the molecular signaling involving RNS was elucidated across plants through the N-end rule for various regulatory substances. In line with transcriptional reprogramming, epigenetic control, and other mechanisms to counteract the sustenance of hypoxic redox, fine-tuned control through hormonal balance with major metabolites such as auxin, ethylene, and abscisic acid was discussed. At the biochemical level, reactions like S-nitrosylation and tyrosine nitration in RNS metabolism were highlighted. A regulatory network involving proteins such as ethylene response factor VII, PIN1, and TIR1, which undergo post-translational modification to manage hypoxia-induced oxidative stress, was also discussed. This review summarizes comprehensive fundamental information on RNS-driven redox signaling and downstream communication to reprogram metabolic cascades for plant tolerance to hypoxia.

Plants coordinate defence against pathogens and herbivores through the crosstalk between salicylic acid (SA) and jasmonic acid (JA) signalling pathways. However, little is known about how plants integrate the phytohormone concentration profiles to shape defence states in complex field environments. Here we show that systematically varying combinatorial SA and JA concentrations in Arabidopsis thaliana reveals 43 distinct combination-specific transcriptional signatures beyond SA-JA antagonism. Leveraging these data, we develop and validate machine-learning-based transcriptomic biomarkers that independently measure the SA and JA response states from gene-expression data. Cerasus humilis is a calcium-rich fruit tree, but how auxin-mediated hormone metabolism is associated with calcium accumulation and partitioning among different fruit tissues remains unclear. In this study, the 'Nongda No. 4' cultivar was treated with exogenous indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), and hormone metabolites and calcium fractions were analyzed in the pedicel, peel, and pulp across three developmental stages (S1-S3). This study also indicated that the predicted cis-regulatory elements in the promoter regions of TaNF-YBs putatively exhibit responsiveness to light, methyl jasmonate (MeJA) and abscisic acid (ABA) responsiveness. Tissue expression profiles revealed that TaNF-YBs exhibit high expression in seeds, which may be associated with grain development and nutrient accumulation. The temporal expression profiles of these family genes under salt stress differed significantly. GO enrichment and in silico protein-protein interaction analyses further suggest that TaNF-YB proteins may potentially activate the transcriptional expression downstream salt-tolerance target genes through heterotrimeric complex binding to their promoter regions, thereby enhancing wheat salt-stress responses. Abstract Background The As2/LOB gene family plays critical roles in regulating plant growth, development, and abiotic stress responses. Despite this gene family has been characterized in multiple plant species, it remained unstudied in the perennial allotetraploid grass Elymus sibiricus , an important species for grassland restoration and forage production on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Results We identified 64 As2/LOB genes in E. sibiricus and systematically characterized their chromosomal distribution, gene structure, conserved motifs, cis-acting elements, and phylogenetic relationships. Phylogenetic analysis classified these proteins into seven distinct subfamilies. Gene structure analysis revealed the presence of conserved domains and motifs characteristic of the As2/LOB family, underscoring both functional conservation and subfamily-specific divergence. Tissue-specific expression profiling across roots, stems, leaves, and spikes at multiple developmental stages revealed pronounced spatial and temporal patterns, with several subfamily members showing preferential enrichment in organs that directly determine plant architecture, nutrient acquisition, and photosynthetic capacity—key traits contributing to forage biomass and yield. In parallel, expression analysis under indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) treatment, a central phytohormone regulating organogenesis and cell elongation, further implicated these genes in auxin-mediated developmental networks underlying vegetative and reproductive growth. Promoter analysis identified numerous hormone-responsive and stress-responsive cis-acting elements, suggesting potential regulatory roles in hormone signalling and environmental adaptation. Chromosomal localization and synteny analysis indicated that the As2/LOB genes were unevenly distributed across the 14 chromosomes and identified multiple syntenic gene pairs, indicating that gene duplication events have contributed to family expansion. In addition, expression profiling under salt, drought, and ABA treatments revealed differential regulation of several members, suggesting their auxiliary roles in stress adaptation that may help stabilize biomass production under unfavorable environments. Conclusion This study provides the first comprehensive genomic resource for the As2/LOB gene family in E. sibiricus , revealing their expansion via duplications and functional diversification in organ development and biomass-related growth. Notably, EsLOB52 was consistently induced across IAA, salt, drought, and ABA treatments, highlighting its potential as a candidate integrator of growth regulation and stress adaptation. abstract

Strawberry is an important fruit crop around the globe. Its yield and quality are fundamentally and closely related to flowering. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the morphological, environmental, hormonal, and molecular regulation of strawberry floral development and the integration of these regulatory layers. Morphologically, strawberry flower differentiation develops from shoot apical meristem transition through sequential floral organ initiation, culminating in the unique pseudocarpic fruit structure. Environmentally, photoperiod, temperature, and light quality are the primary signals governing strawberry flowering. In seasonal-flowering genotypes, this module typically shifts the balance toward the TFL1-FD-14-3-3 repressor complex, suppressing floral identity genes and repressing flowering. In perpetual-flowering F. vesca genotypes, loss of functional FvTFL1 shifts the balance toward the FT-FD-14-3-3 activator complex, promoting continuous flowering. In cultivated octoploid strawberry, the genetic basis of perpetual flowering is more complex and involves additional loci beyond TFL1. Hormonally, gibberellins, cytokinins, auxin, abscisic acid, ethylene, and jasmonic acid modulate the core photoperiodic regulation at multiple nodes. Molecularly, these signals converge on integrated networks in which the CO-FT1-SOC1-TFL1 module plays a central role, auxin signaling directly activates floral meristem identity genes, and octoploid-specific regulatory features add further complexity. This review provides an integrated overview for future research reference and breeding of strawberry flowering.

Abstract Background Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone controlling development, stress responses, and senescence, yet its quantitative measurement remains methodologically heterogeneous across plant research. Here, we present a unified experimental workflow that combines gas chromatography with flame ionization detection (GC–FID) and laser‑based photoacoustic spectroscopy (PAS) for the quantification of endogenous ethylene production in plants. Although both techniques are widely used, a direct experimental comparison using identical biological samples has not been reported previously. Results Using Arabidopsis seedlings and wheat leaf segments, we demonstrate that GC–FID and PAS values are offset by a system-dependent proportional factor while following highly consistent dose‑response trends across a broad range of ethylene‑modulating treatments. Across all compounds and concentrations, ethylene values measured by both methods were strongly correlated. GC–FID provided superior linearity at high ethylene outputs, whereas PAS offered high sensitivity for low‑to‑moderate ethylene levels and faster sample throughput. The workflow defines a consistent set of experimental parameters, including delayed treatment application, normalization of ethylene production to plant fresh weight (FW), and minimization of biomass‑related artefacts. Applying this approach, we systematically evaluated inhibitors and inducers of ethylene biosynthesis and signaling, including aminoethoxyvinylglycine (AVG), aminooxyacetic acid (AOA), 2‑aminoisobutyric acid (AIB), 2‑picolinic acid (2‑PA), 1-aminocyclopropane‑1‑carboxylic acid (ACC), silver thiosulfate (STS), thidiazuron (TDZ), ethephon (ETH), and mebendazole (MEB). The data reveal pronounced species‑specific sensitivities and clear toxicity thresholds for several compounds. Importantly, the parallel ethylene measurement workflow is compatible with downstream LC–MS/MS based phytohormone profiling. Correlation analysis of ethylene, its precursor ACC, multiple phytohormones, and FW is consistent with ACC availability as a significant determinant of ethylene production in Arabidopsis and wheat, while many apparent hormonal associations reflect indirect stress or growth effects rather than direct regulatory coupling. Conclusion This study provides a robust and extensible platform for ethylene quantification and interpretation across plant systems. The parallel GC–FID/PAS approach improves cross‑validation of measurements and enables direct integration of ethylene production into broader phytohormonal analyses, facilitating reliable comparison of ethylene‑related studies across laboratories and plant species.

BackgroundSaxifraga stolonifera Curtis is a shade-tolerant, variegated-leaf herb with ornamental and medicinal value that naturally displays three stable leaf phenotypes: green, white-variegated, and purple-variegated. Abstract Background Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and urease-producing bacteria (UPB) are common rhizosphere microorganisms in cadmium (Cd)-contaminated soils, but their effects on maize growth and Cd tolerance across substrates remain unclear. Purpose To evaluate the effects of single inoculation with AMF or UPB and dual inoculation (BF) on maize growth, physiology, and Cd tolerance under sand and soil culture, and to clarify the substrate-dependent physiological mechanisms. Methods Sand- and soil-culture experiments under 25 mg kg⁻¹ Cd stress were conducted. The treatments included single inoculation with AMF or UPB and dual inoculation (BF). Maize growth, physiology, and Cd tolerance were evaluated. Results In sand culture, BF increased plant height, shoot and belowground biomass, and stomatal conductance by 47–75%, while AMF increased root length and root surface area by 274% and 100% and reduced shoot Cd content by 57%; BF increased shoot and belowground Cd accumulation by 280% and 77%. In soil culture, UPB increased plant height by 16%, and AMF, UPB, and BF increased shoot biomass by 47–62%. UPB enhanced photosynthetic rate and stomatal conductance by 28% and 51%; BF increased stomatal conductance by 44% and decreased transpiration rate by 27%. AMF increased shoot K and belowground P by 61% and 45% and reduced shoot Cd content by 20%; BF reduced shoot Cd content by 16%; AMF increased belowground Cd accumulation by 31%. Inoculation reduced MDA content, enhanced SOD, POD, and CAT activities, and modulated IAA, ABA, ZR, and GA levels, with AMF and UPB interactions. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) indicated that in sand culture, AMF and UPB mainly affected photosynthesis by regulating endogenous hormones, thereby reducing maize Cd content; in soil culture, AMF and UPB treatments exerted direct negative effects on Cd content, whereas the hormonal pathway indirectly reduced Cd content per unit biomass, mainly through photosynthetic improvement and growth dilution. Conclusion Overall, AMF and UPB reduce Cd and enhance maize Cd tolerance via photosynthetic physiology, antioxidant defense, and hormone modulation, with substrate-dependent co-inoculation effects.

Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with 2.00 mg/L 6-benzyladenine (6-BA), 0.20 mg/L 1-naphthaleneacetic acid (NAA), and 0.05 mg/L kinetin (KT) yielded a proliferation coefficient of 8.16. Half-strength MS medium (1/2MS) was suitable for rooting, and 0.50 mg/L indole-3-butyric acid (IBA) produced a rooting rate of 92.22%. Under the selected culture conditions, soluble sugar content generally increased during shoot proliferation, soluble protein content peaked on day 14, and SOD and POD levels peaked on day 21. During rooting, soluble sugar content declined after day 7, whereas soluble protein content and SOD levels reached high values on day 14. During the middle and later culture periods, treated plantlets generally had higher IAA and lower ABA contents than the controls at both stages. Comparisons among formulations showed that the treatment favorable for proliferation had relatively high soluble sugar and ZR contents, whereas the treatment favorable for rooting had relatively low contents of both. The selected growth regulator concentrations were suitable within the tested ranges for this genotype. Their applicability to other C. officinarum genotypes requires further validation.

The work proposed a correlative inhibition (CI) model based on positive feedback (PF) between sugars (Sug) and cytokinis (CKs) - CK activates Sug uploading to sink organs, and Sug increases CK content and activates CK signalling. This creates an unstable PF system capable of triggering the development of dominant and suppressed shoots on the same plant. The predictions of the Sug-CK model were tested on two-branched pea seedlings. Sug deficiency (removal of part of the cotyledons) and CK deficiency (treatment with an inhibitor of CK synthesis) in accordance with the model increased the occurrence of unequal-branched plants. Surprisingly, auxin was found to be inactive in the regulation of CI. In the apical buds of lateral shoots, a Sug deficiency reduced the CK signal, as measured by the expression of PsRR5 gene, whilst inhibition of CK synthesis reduced Sug accumulation, thereby confirming the presence of PF between CK and Sug. A deficiency of Sug enhanced the effect of a CK deficiency in reducing CK status, explaining the synergistic effect of both deficiencies on CI. A deficiency of strigolactones (SL) in the rms5 and rms1 mutants and SL insensitivity in the rms4 mutant completely abolished the effects of CK and Sug deficiencies on CI. It was demonstrated on the rms5 mutant that a CK deficiency did not affect Sug levels thus explaining the insensitivity to CK-Sug deficiencies in SL mutants. The BRANCHED1 (BRC1) gene is an important regulator of plant branching, and its absence in the brc1 mutant resulted in a lack of response to Sug deficiency with regard to both CI and CK status. It has thus been shown that SL signalling and the BRC1 gene are involved in the Sug-CK interaction, thereby playing a role in the regulation of CI.

Main conclusionChemical activation of ABA signaling via synthetic agonists provides a reversible, high-precision strategy to optimize wheat water-use efficiency by coupling persistent antitranspirant effects with the metabolic reinforcement of carbohydrate reserves. The phytohormone abscisic acid (ABA) and its PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors are central targets for improving crop drought tolerance. In hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum), the actual number of ABA receptors (TaPYLs) has been a matter of debate, ranging from 26 to 38. This study refines this classification, demonstrating that 12 putative TaPYLs belong to the Bet v/START/Polyketide cyclase superfamily, but lack key structural features of functional ABA receptors. Indeed, structural and bioinformatic analyses confirm that their ligand-binding cavities cannot accommodate ABA and lack key residues for ABA binding. As a result, whereas TaPYL1, TaPYL4, and TaPYL6 mediate ABA-dependent inhibition of PP2Cs, the TraesCS3B02G160200 putative receptor does not. Therefore, wheat has only 26 potential TaPYL ABA receptors. Given the biotechnological potential of the ABA pathway, we investigated its chemical activation using the synthetic receptor agonist iSB09. This compound is perceived by highly expressed TaPYLs and induces a more persistent antitranspirant effect than exogenous ABA. Plants treated with iSB09 consumed approximately 25% less water over 15 days without incurring a biomass penalty, resulting in significantly higher water productivity. Beyond regulating transpiration, agonist treatment increased fructan and starch levels compared with controls. A short-term RNA-seq experiment revealed that ABA treatment triggers a coordinated reprogramming of carbohydrate metabolism genes, including the upregulation of genes involved in the biosynthesis of protective osmolytes (fructans and raffinose) and starch, coupled with the downregulation of genes involved in starch mobilization. In summary, this work provides a clarified census of the wheat TaPYL family, establishes chemical activation of ABA signaling as an effective strategy to boost water-use efficiency, and suggests that the reinforcement of reserve and protective carbohydrate pathways is a key metabolic mechanism linked to ABA signaling.

These outputs influence microbial sensing and resource use, while host immune and metabolic conditions help regulate colonization and persistence. The potential health effects of concurrent exposure to ozone, PM2.5, and heat remain largely unexplored. Triple exposure can overwhelm host compensatory systems via three interrelated mechanisms: increasing biologically effective exposure doses, reducing host tolerance, and converging upon shared defensive signaling cascades. This interplay elicits emergent health effects that cannot be inferred from single or pairwise exposure scenarios. Future studies should combine environmentally relevant chronic low-dose coexposure models, multiomics approaches, and longitudinal population studies to identify susceptibility profiles, clarify interactive toxicological mechanisms, and improve risk assessment and targeted prevention strategies under the combined pressures of air pollution and climate change.

The NLRP3 inflammasome is a critical innate immune sensor detecting diverse pathogen- and damage-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs/DAMPs). Its activation triggers the maturation and release of the proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18, as well as pyroptotic cell death. Since dysregulated NLRP3 activity drives various autoinflammatory and metabolic diseases, it represents a major therapeutic target. This review provides an updated framework of NLRP3 activation mechanisms, emphasizing the roles of the NACHT and LRR domains in NEK7 recruitment and the PYD domain in ASC recruitment. We identify specific residues within these domains to guide docking-based studies. Furthermore, this review highlights the principal chemical scaffolds of emerging small-molecule NLRP3 inhibitors, both synthetic and natural products, with a focus on clinical candidates and pharmacological profiles. Special attention is given to plant-derived natural products as a source of NLRP3 drug discovery, which has expanded the inhibitor chemical space. Finally, we address future challenges, such as targeting upstream activation signals (e.g., ROS or oxidized DNA interactions), and designing dual inhibitors for multiple inflammasomes (e.g., AIM2, NLRP1, NLRC4) to mitigate inflammasome crosstalk. 6.0 Mycorrhizal evolution restructures forest ecosystems
Yamawo A, Shinohara N, Kadowaki K … Utsumi S.
preprintAbiotic stressGrowthTrees and woody plantsEcoEvoRxiv · 2026-11-13
matched: mycorrhiz*, symbio*, defense, nutrient*, seed*, tree, trees, ectomycorrhiz*
abstract

Mutualisms are key drivers of species diversification and biodiversity, yet their comprehensive role in shaping contemporary ecosystems remains poorly understood. Mycorrhizal symbioses (Arbuscular mycorrhiza [AM] and Ectomycorrhizal [EcM]) are among the most ecologically important interactions on Earth, driving the origin and maintenance of terrestrial biodiversity. Nearly all tree species associate with these fungi; AM symbiosis, the ancient form, dominates tropical forests, while the later-emerging EcM symbiosis, though taxonomically narrow, primarily influences temperate forests. Previous studies have shown that mycorrhizal type is associated with both tree population density and forest spatial organization. At the population level, EcM trees tend to attain higher local densities than AM trees. At the forest-community level, EcM-rich forests exhibit stronger spatial structuring, characterized by greater conspecific aggregation than the dispersed distributions typically observed in AM-dominated forests. In this paper, we propose the Ecosystem Regime Restructuring by Mycorrhizal Symbiosis (ERRM) hypothesis. Here, we defome am ecosystem regime as the large-scale organization of ecosystems characterized by dominant spatial structures, trophic interactions, and trait syndromes. This hypothesis posits that the evolutionary shifts in mycorrhizal type from AM to EcM have widely altered ecosystem spatial structure, thereby reshaping tree macroevolutionary patterns, driving large-scale ecosystem reorganization, and creating distinct ecological and evolutionary contexts. Dispersed AM trees typically favor long-range biotic seed dispersal and biotic pollination. Clustered EcM trees, conversely, favor wind pollination and short-range wind dispersal. This suggests joint evolution between mycorrhizal type and reproductive/dispersal modes. Spatial structure also influences plant defense strategies: clustered EcM trees may tend to display a higher carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and carbon-based quantitative defenses. AM trees may be associated with higher nutrient content and qualitative chemical defenses like alkaloids. These contrasting defense strategies may reflect differences in herbivore encounter rates determined by the spatial structure of AM and EcM communities. Furthermore, the dense, stable resource environment provided by EcM clusters facilitates the evolution of specialized herbivores. We present this novel hypothesis with an empirical dataset partially supporting it. Finally, we argue that the ERRM hypothesis provides the fundamental framework toward a new understanding of the present ecosystem regime with an integrative approach combining phylogenetic analysis, macroecology, and experimental studies.

Drought and salt stress impose osmotic and ionic challenges on plant roots, with drought reducing soil water potential and salt imposing additional ionic toxicity beyond osmotic stress, driving the plastic remodeling of root system architecture (RSA). Abscisic acid (ABA) is a central hormone regulating root adaptability, and its signaling coordinates adaptive responses of roots across multiple time scales through the SNF1-related protein kinase 2 (SnRK2) family kinases. This review systematically summarizes the temporal coding mechanisms of the ABA-SnRK2 signaling network underlying root adaptation to osmotic stress. We propose that plant roots achieve a dynamic balance between short-term defense and long-term adaptation through the coordinated activities of different SnRK2 subgroups along the temporal axis. This proposed "balance point" of temporal coding is shaped by multiple temporal readouts. We also review how crosstalk between ABA and other hormones such as auxin fine-tunes root plasticity. abstract

Salinity stress represents a significant environmental challenge that affects plant growth, resulting in adverse impacts on crop productivity and overall yield. Salt accumulation in plants affects cellular homeostasis and provokes osmotic and ionic imbalance. It stimulates higher reactive oxygen species (ROS) production leading to oxidative stress damage and eventual cellular dysfunction. Beneficial microorganisms like plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, endophytic fungi, and rhizosphere-associated microbes have recently emerged as resources for sustainable solutions to enhance plant resiliency against salinity stress. Their effects can involve osmotic adjustment, ion sequestration, oxidative-stress mitigation, phytohormone regulation, and rhizosphere-mediated stress buffering. The mechanisms to impart such benefits may include improved nutrients acquisition, assist in osmotic regulation, modulation of phytohormones signaling, and maintenance of cellular ion homeostasis. Often, beneficial microorganisms carry the potential to trigger both enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant defense mechanisms. These responses contribute to oxidative-stress mitigation, yet, their interpretation requires contemplation of fine balance between oxidative damage and plant responses. For example, selected microbial inoculation studies have reported changes in the activity of crucial antioxidant enzymes, like superoxide dismutase, ascorbate peroxidase, catalase, and glutathione reductase. However, the magnitude and the direction of these responses are context dependent. Multi-omics approaches, including amplicon and shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, host transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, have expanded our understanding of the taxa, genes, transcripts, proteins, and metabolites associated with plant-microbe interactions under salinity. Therefore, here an effort has been made to present the evidential support for reported microbial effects and their proposed mechanisms of salt tolerance, with a focus on enzymatic and non-enzymatic defense mechanisms and the learnings of multi-omics studies. Frontier integrative mechanisms, including microbiome engineering, synthetic microbial consortia, and systems biology frameworks, are discussed for cultivating climate-resilient crops and sustainable agricultural systems in the salt-affected environments.

Drought is one of the major constraints limiting legume productivity, impairing plant growth, biological nitrogen fixation, and seed nutritional quality. The increasing frequency and intensity of water scarcity have intensified the search for sustainable strategies to improve crop resilience. Bacteria isolated from extreme environments have been proposed as candidate bioinoculants because adaptations to desiccation, salinity, or extreme temperatures may provide traits relevant to plant performance under water deficit. However, most of these isolates are extremotolerant rather than extremophilic sensu stricto, and much of the supporting evidence derives from stresses other than drought. The objective of this review is to synthesize current knowledge on the mechanisms through which extremophilic and extremotolerant bacteria may contribute to drought tolerance in legumes, using explicit operational definitions for these microbial categories and for drought, and a four-tier evidence classification applied at the level of individual studies. Candidate mechanisms include exopolysaccharide- and biofilm-mediated rhizosphere water retention, modulation of root architecture and auxin/ethylene balance through ACC deaminase activity, osmolyte accumulation, antioxidant responses, nutrient mobilization, maintenance of nodulation and biological nitrogen fixation, and regulation of host stress-responsive genes. Direct evidence, defined as extremophilic or extremotolerant strains evaluated in legumes under soil water deficit, is restricted to a small number of studies, whereas a large proportion of the literature relies on salinity, heat, or PEG-induced osmotic stress, non-legume hosts, genomic potential, or in vitro assays. We also discuss constraints that may limit the use of these bacteria, including rhizosphere colonization, persistence, and competitiveness against native microbiota under non-extreme conditions. Current findings provide plausible mechanisms and proof-of-concept results, but they do not yet demonstrate reliable field performance of extremophile-derived inoculants in legume production. Strain-level characterization, standardized drought protocols, and multi-environment field validation are required to establish their agronomic value.

Salt stress is a major constraint on rice production because it inhibits plant growth and reduces yield. Although millimeter-wave (MMW) seed priming was reported to improve plant performance under environmental stress, the molecular mechanisms underlying its effects remain largely unknown. This study examined whether MMW seed priming improves early rice performance under salt stress and characterized associated changes in the root proteome. Rice seeds were irradiated with MMW, and morphological traits were evaluated under 150 mM NaCl as salt stress for 2 days. Based on morphological results, rice seeds were irradiated with 20 mW for 20 min. Root proteins were analyzed based on the growth responses. Among 6307 proteins analyzed with label-free proteomics, selected proteomic observations were further examined by immunoblotting, gene-expression analysis, and starch measurements. MMW irradiation improved seed germination and alleviated salt-induced inhibition of root growth. Proteomic analysis showed that proteins associated with carbohydrate metabolism and endoplasmic-reticulum function were markedly affected by MMW irradiation. Glutathione reductase and ascorbate peroxidase accumulated under salt stress and further increased following MMW irradiation. Calreticulin and calcium-dependent protein kinase were also increased in abundance by MMW irradiation under salt stress. In addition, soluble starch content, which declined under salt stress, was attenuated the salt-associated reduction by MMW irradiation. These findings extend molecular studies of MMW-mediated salt-stress responses to the rice root proteome and identify candidate proteins and biological processes associated with the improved salt-tolerant phenotype. BackgroundSoil salinization constrains crop yield and ecological restoration. Endophytic bacteria can promote plant growth and enhance tolerance to abiotic stresses. Using salt-sensitive cucumber as a model, we systematically evaluated six endophytic bacterial strains for salt-tolerance, including Pseudomonas fulva PY-1, Kosakonia cowanii Cya-1, Bacillus stercoris Cya-2, Serratia marcescens QP-1, Raoultella terrigena Ma-1 and Novosphingobium capsulatum Ly-1, and investigated their potential mechanisms in alleviating salt-induced damage.ResultsAll six bacterial strains were able to tolerate high salinity (1 mol/L NaCl) in vitro and significantly mitigated salt stress damage to cucumber seedlings under 250 mmol/L NaCl. Multi-omics analysis (microbiome, transcriptome, and metabolome) revealed that these strains influenced the rhizosphere microecological niche, leading to increasing abundance of salt-tolerant microbial taxa and the establishment of a stress-resilient community structure. For example, in the Cya-2 treatment group, the relative abundance of the genus Pseudomonas increased by an average of 5.87%, and that of genus Microvirga peaked at 9.92%. Based on the salt-alleviating efficacy and distinct response strategies, Pseudomonas fulva PY-1 and Serratia marcescens QP-1 were selected as representative strains. Both strains significantly activated cucumber ABC transporters and glycerophospholipid metabolism pathways. The key divergence between the two strains was that PY-1 treatment drove greater upregulation of α-linolenic acid metabolism genes, and broadly modulated plant hormone signal transduction; additionally, PY-1 was associated with activation of bacterial teichoic acid biosynthesis pathways. In contrast, QP-1 treatment showed enrichment in carbon and nitrogen metabolism pathways (galactose, starch/sucrose metabolism, and arginine biosynthesis). QP-1 was correlated with bacterial alkaloid biosynthesis as well as degradation pathways of glutathione, arachidonic acid, and aminobenzoate. Furthermore, exogenous application of three bacterial-derived metabolites (gambogic acid, dihydrocoumarin, and 2-aminonicotinic acid) and one cucumber-produced metabolite (triptolide) significantly alleviated salt damage in cucumber, indicating the possible bioactivity of these compounds in enhancing salt tolerance.ConclusionsThis work identified six bacterial strains and four bioactive metabolites capable of significantly alleviating salt-induced plant damage. Integrative multi-omics correlation analysis, we further proposed a hypothetical "microbe-metabolite-gene" regulatory framework to understand the synergistic interactions among endophytes, metabolites and plant host genes, which may collectively contribute to plant salt tolerance, laying a foundation for future targeted verification. Beyond providing candidate microbial strains and bioactive compounds for developing plant stress-tolerance enhancers, this study generates a rich multi‑omics dataset to support further hypothesis‑based research. Soil salinity severely limits plant growth and productivity through osmotic stress, ion toxicity, and excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Although TIFY proteins regulate plant responses to environmental stresses, their roles in salt tolerance in foxtail millet (Setaria italica) remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized SiTIFY9 (Seita.9G51810) through phylogenetic analysis, expression profiling, subcellular localization, transcriptional activation assays, stable overexpression, physiological measurements, and transcriptome sequencing. SiTIFY9 clustered with rice OsTIFY11a/OsJAZ9, localized predominantly to the nucleus, and exhibited no autonomous transcriptional activation activity in yeast. Under salt stress, SiTIFY9-overexpressing plants showed reduced hydrogen peroxide and malondialdehyde accumulation, increased catalase and peroxidase activities, and enhanced proline accumulation compared with wild-type plants. Overexpression also restricted Na+ accumulation, promoted K+ retention, and increased the K+/Na+ ratio, indicating improved ionic homeostasis. Transcriptome analysis revealed extensive transcriptional changes associated with stress responses, redox regulation, ion transport, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, and secondary metabolism. RT-qPCR further confirmed altered expression of genes involved in ion transport, osmoprotection, transcriptional regulation, and stress defense. Independently, SiTIFY9-overexpressing plants flowered 14-16 days earlier than wild-type plants under non-saline conditions, suggesting an additional role in flowering-time regulation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that SiTIFY9 overexpression enhances salt tolerance by improving antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, and ionic homeostasis, accompanied by transcriptional reprogramming of stress-responsive pathways. Furthermore, its association with earlier flowering suggests a potential developmental function. This study identifies SiTIFY9 as a promising candidate for further investigation of salt-stress tolerance and flowering-time regulation in foxtail millet.

Functional assays indicate that HON4 and HON5 impair the ability of ABFs to activate downstream stress-responsive genes. Collectively, these findings establish HON4 and HON5 as novel nuclear co-repressors that attenuate ABA-mediated stress signaling by inhibiting the transcriptional activity of ABFs, revealing a previously unrecognized chromatin-associated layer of regulation in plant stress responses.

Drought is a major constraint to cowpea productivity, but its effects on root-associated endophytic fungi remain poorly understood. This study investigated how drought influences cowpea root endophytic fungal communities and evaluated the plant growth-promoting potential of cultured fungal endophytes. Internal transcribed spacer (ITS) amplicon sequencing revealed that drought significantly altered fungal community composition. Several fungal taxa, including Aspergillus and Chaetomium, showed numerical differences in abundance under drought, although these taxon-specific differences were not significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In parallel, 13 fungal endophytes were isolated from drought-treated cowpea roots and evaluated for plant growth-promoting traits. The isolates differed in 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC) deaminase activity and presumptive indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) production, and several promoted wheat seedling growth under polyethylene glycol (PEG)-induced osmotic stress. Selected isolates also enhanced okra pollen germination under osmotic stress. Further evaluation through direct inoculation of cowpea under drought is needed to determine their potential for improving crop performance under water-limited conditions.

Upland cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) is a global cash crop cultivated extensively for its high-quality fiber and oil-rich seeds. Several gene families are involved in the regulatory pathways that enable plants to acclimate to adverse abiotic stresses. Although GhSOS3 has previously been associated with salt-alkali stress responses in cotton, a family level genomic characterization of SOS3-like genes in the allotetraploid G. hirsutum genome has not been reported. This analysis identified five putative GhSOS3 genes. The encoded proteins showed conserved EF-hand-related motifs, with differences in gene structure, predicted physicochemical properties, and motif composition. Putative abscisic acid-responsive (ABRE), salicylic acid-responsive (SARE), drought stress-responsive (DSRE) and gibberellin-responsive (GRE) elements predicted in the promoters suggest that the GhSOS3 genes may be transcriptionally responsive to abiotic stress-related signals; however, these predictions require experimental validation. Experimentally, qPCR analysis showed stress- and time-dependent changes in the transcript abundance of GhSOS3-2 and GhSOS3-3 under drought, salt, and heat treatments in three cotton genotypes, indicating differential transcriptional responses to these stress conditions. Heavy metal (HM) pollution is a major threat to terrestrial ecosystems. Addressing it requires identifying native plant species that tolerate HMs while maintaining physiological function. This study evaluated the physiological responses, antioxidant defense mechanisms, and phytoremediation potential of the high-Andean species Adesmia subterranea Clos under cadmium (Cd 3, 4.5, and 6 mg L-1) and mercury (Hg 0.8, 1.2, and 1.6 mg L-1) in a semi-hydroponic system. Exposure to Cd reduced survival and decreased biomass in a concentration-dependent manner, whereas Hg did not affect survival and reduced biomass only at 0.8 mg L-1. Both metals were efficiently taken up (BCF > 1); Cd was consistently retained in roots (TF -1). Cd and Hg exposure induced oxidative stress, evidenced by increased H2O2 accumulation and lipid peroxidation, which was accompanied by activation of antioxidant defenses. The APX activity and GSH levels increased significantly, while CAT showed a metal-specific response. These results indicate coordinated regulation of enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant pathways to maintain redox homeostasis under HM stress. Overall, these results provide a preliminary indication of the potential of A. subterranea for phytostabilization in metal-contaminated Andean ecosystems.

Abstract Background and aims Soil salinity disrupts photosynthetic functions through increased oxidative stress. Methods Mustard plants were treated with 10 μM MeJA applied individually or in combination with 200 mg S kg⁻¹ soil or 200 mg nS kg⁻¹ soil under 100 mM NaCl. Antioxidant and proline metabolism, stomatal architecture, cell viability and photosynthesis and growth were evaluated. Results Salinity increased H₂O₂ and TBARS levels resulting in reduced photosynthesis and plant growth. The combined MeJA and nS application alleviated salinity stress more prominently than their individual applications by reducing H₂O₂ and TBARS levels, enhancing the activities of antioxidant enzymes and AsA–GSH cycle metabolite pools. This coordinated response preserved stomatal integrity and cell viability and increased net photosynthesis and dry matter accumulation. Furthermore, MeJA+nS enhanced proline accumulation through increased activity of pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthetase (P5CS) and γ-glutamyl kinase (GK) and suppressed proline oxidase (PROX) activity. Conclusion MeJA and nS application together alleviated salinity stress more conspicuously through coordinated regulation of ion homeostasis, antioxidant defense and proline metabolism, maintaining stomatal architecture, photosynthesis and growth. This study evaluated the individual and combined effects of Eucalyptus-derived biochar and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) on the growth, physiology, nutrient acquisition, and drought tolerance of Cicer arietinum. It also suppressed AMF colonisation, spore abundance, mycelial development, vesicle formation, arbuscule abundance, and root colonisation percentage.
